en: Commentary on the Verses on the Ritual for the Novice’s Training in the Precepts, by the Śramaṇa Shi Hongzan of Dinghu in Yue Dong; annotated at Zai Qi.
Commentary on the Verses on the Ritual for the Novice’s Training in the Precepts.
There are two kinds of śrāmaṇeras. First, those who resemble śrāmaṇeras in form: this refers to those who have shaved their hair and beards but have not yet received the ten precepts.
Although they share the same outward appearance, because they lack the precepts, they are not true śrāmaṇeras. Second, those who resemble śrāmaṇeras in dharma:
this refers to those who have received the dharma of the ten precepts from a teacher. This consists of three types: first, those from the age of seven to thirteen.

From the age of seven until thirteen, one is called a *kū-ō* (crow-chaser) śrāmaṇera. Because they are too young to undertake other duties, they are only tasked with driving away crows and birds so as to avoid defiling the kitchen and disturbing the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of the monks;
by causing them to produce even a slight degree of goodness, the offerings of the faithful (*śraddhā-dakṣiṇā*) are thereby rendered pure.
From the age of fourteen until nineteen, one is called a *ō-hō* (conforming to the Dharma) śrāmaṇera, meaning that they are in accordance with the Dharma.

They are able to endure toil while serving their preceptors and cultivate morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Third, from the age of twenty until seventy, they are called *nāma-śrāmaṇeras*.
This means that although they have reached twenty years of age and should receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), their faculties and nature are dull and obtuse;
thus, they are unable to uphold all the precepts at once, or they entered the monastic life late, such that their age has already exceeded the [standard] for a *śrāmaṇera*.
*Śrāmaṇera*. Although their age may equal that of a *bhikṣu*, they rank below those who have received the ten precepts; therefore, they are called "name-only śrāmaṇeras.
Here, we select those who share the same outward form to include those who share the same dharma. *Śikṣā* means to study and practice.

This refers to when one has first received the śrāmaṇera precepts and is not yet able to extensively read the ten *vinayas* and the complete sūtras to investigate their essential points; one must first study these verses, as they serve as the key to the *vinaya*. *Śīla* (precepts) refers to...
The ten precepts are the *vinaya*. "Ritual" (*yi*) refers to majestic deportment (*vīryāpatha*); "rules" (*gui*) refer to the standards and models of conduct.

This means that these disciplinary rules (*śīla-vinaya*) serve as the standards and models for transcending the world; thus, a sutra says: "The *prātimokṣa* is your teacher. This is precisely what that means.
As for the *gāthās*, they are essentially a versification of the *Śrāmaṇera-saṃvara-sūtra* along with the texts concerning the methods for serving one's teacher and so forth,
composed as verses (*gāthā*) to facilitate recitation by beginners. According to the sūtras and śāstras,
a single verse may consist of thirty-two syllables, twenty-eight syllables, twenty syllables, or ten [syllables].
Six characters constitute one verse. In this present ritual manual, twenty characters constitute one verse, totaling one hundred and seventeen verses.
These all recount the words of the Sūtras and Vinaya; they are not based on my own arbitrary views.

Since the Vinaya was personally ordained by the Buddha, it is something that even Bodhisattvas and Arhats—lesser sages—cannot presume to alter, let alone allow ordinary, ignorant people to dare to do so.
A presumptuous deliberation:
The son of Śākyamuni’s perfect enlightenment, whose name is Rāhula, is foremost in his secret conduct;
one should diligently emulate and learn from him.
This verse provides the background for the origin [of this work], clarifying the causal practices of the Venerable One so that people may emulate his former footsteps.
In the Sanskrit language, Śākya is the clan name; in the Chinese language, it means "Capable Benevolent One. His title is Muni, which in the Chinese language means "Silent Sage."
There are briefly five surnames: Gautama, Ādityavaṃśa (Solar Lineage), Ikṣvāku (Sugarcane), Śākiya, and Śākya.
According to accounts of the past, King Mahāmuni abandoned his kingdom to follow the sage Gautama and study the Way; thus, he took Gautama as his surname.

Later, encountering a perilous situation, drops of his blood fell to the earth and formed eggs. Incubated by the sun, two sons were born, who consequently took Ādityavaṃśa (Solar Lineage) as their surname. They were raised at...
In the midst of a sugarcane grove, his lineage was again that of Ikṣvāku, passed down through successive generations until King Māndhātṛ.

When he banished his four sons from the kingdom, they reached the side of the Snow Mountains and dwelt in the Great Straight Forest (Śālavatīvana) of Śākya. Having established their borders and founded a state, they thus took the surname Śākya.
Later, when the father-king heard that his sons had established a kingdom, he sighed three times and said: "My sons are truly capable and benevolent."

Because his clan was Śākya, he is thus named. Although one hundred generations have passed since the time of the Tathāgata, and although there were five clans, this is actually one of the clans of the Kṣatriya royal lineage.
As for the term "Perfectly Awakened" (Sambuddha): his teaching of the Dharma is without error, which is why it is called "Perfect" (Samyak).
To emerge from the dream of birth and death is called awakening (*bodhi*). Furthermore, awakening possesses three meanings:

self-awakening, awakening others, and the perfection of awakened practice. These are the epithets of the Tathāgata; it is the designation for Great Awakening (*mahābodhi*), wherein practice is fulfilled and fruition is perfected.
"Son" (*putra*) refers to the noble descendant of Śākyamuni Tathāgata. "Jue" (厥) means "that" (*tat*); it is also a refined term used as a particle.
In the Sanskrit language he is called Rāhula; in the Chinese language it means "obscuration" (fùzhàng), and is also translated as "seizing the sun.
Formerly, when the Tathāgata was a crown prince, his father the King, fearing that he would renounce the world, took him three wives:
the first named Gopī, the second Yaśodharā, and the third Mṛgajā. However, because the Buddha does not follow the way of husband and wife, he had no offspring.
Later, he traveled through the four gates and beheld old age, sickness, and death; observing that the world is impermanent, he requested his father’s permission to leave the household life.
His father said, "You have no offspring; you would cut off my dynastic succession. If you were to have a son, I would allow you to leave the household life.
The Prince then pointed to Yaśodharā’s womb with his finger, and she immediately became pregnant. Thereupon, the Prince crossed the city wall at midnight and practiced asceticism.
For six years, Yaśodharā also practiced asceticism within the royal palace;

consequently, the fetus remained hidden within her womb, and it was only after six years that he was born, hence he was called "The Obstructed" (Āvarita). Furthermore, because an asura obstructs the sun and moon with his hand, he is named Rāhu;
since the Venerable One was born precisely when such an asura was seizing the sun, he was given this name accordingly.
The Venerable One was handsome in countenance, his body golden-hued, his head shaped like a parasol, his nose high, long, and straight, and his arms reaching down past his knees.
His limbs were without defect and his faculties were fully intact. When he had grown to maturity, the Buddha requested that he go forth from the household life.
The King, his father, would not permit it. Yaśodharā was about to ascend to the upper story when Maudgalyāyana flew through the air and brought her to the presence of the Buddha.
The Buddha immediately entrusted her to Śāriputra to ordain her as a disciple and conferred upon her the ten precepts.
Among all the śrāmaṇeras, Rāhula was the first to receive the precepts. Had the Venerable One not left the household life, his rank would have been that of an Iron-Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin).
The Wheel-Turning King ruled over the single continent of Jambudvīpa; he left the household life, became an Arhat, and realized the fruit of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
The Buddha commanded sixteen Arhats not to enter *nirvāṇa*, but to protect and uphold the True Dharma and serve as fields of merit for the world.
The Venerable One was one of them; therefore, he still remains in the world today. If there is a donor who provides food as an offering to the Sangha, [the Venerable One will appear].
He then transformed his body to appear before them, enabling the donor to obtain a supreme reward.

Regarding "foremost in secret practice," various sutras sometimes describe him as foremost in patience (*kṣānti*) and sometimes as foremost in ethical discipline (*śīla*); each of these designations has its own specific causes and conditions.
I shall not record this in detail here. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the Buddha bestowed a prediction upon him, saying: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood;
your name shall be Tāpitasaptaratnapuṣpa Tathāgata. He further spoke in verse: "When I was a crown prince, Rāhula was my eldest son;
now that I have attained the Way of the Buddha, he receives the Dharma as my Dharma-son. In a future age... [he shall see...]
Under immeasurable billions of Buddhas, he was always their eldest son, single-mindedly seeking the Buddha-way.
Rāhula’s secret practices—only I can know them. Now appearing as my eldest son, he demonstrates this to all sentient beings.
His immeasurable billions of merits are beyond counting; abiding securely in the Buddha-dharma, he seeks the unsurpassed path. He is truly venerable.
These individuals were originally bodhisattvas, yet they manifested as śrāvakas; therefore, their subtle and secret wondrous practices can be known only by a Buddha.
Now, because their traces conceal their fundamental nature, they are called "secret practices" (*guhyacaryā*) and also termed "concealed obstructions.

Having become sons of the Buddha, they are able to shoulder the family legacy, thereby manifesting their future attainment of Buddhahood; for this reason, these practices are placed at the beginning. One should diligently emulate and study them.
That is to say, one should emulate and learn from them; patience and the observance of the precepts are the foremost of secret practices.
Shaving the head and donning the saffron robes, one receives and upholds the ten precepts;

this is called being a *śrāmaṇera*, the initial foundation for entering the Path. In foreign lands they are called *śrāmaṇera*; in the language of China, they are named "those who have stilled their passions" (*xīcí*).
Quelling the evils of body and speech, Compassionately aiding all living beings.

The first verse derives its name from receiving the Dharma; the subsequent verse explains the name to reveal its meaning. Furthermore, the first verse distinguishes the characteristics of the mind from worldly forms;
the subsequent verse clarifies that the name is derived from the mind. As for "shaving the hair and wearing plain robes," this refers to the shaven head and the square-cut monastic garment.
It is the same for the Tathāgata’s *maṇḍala* robe (*maṇicīvara*). This refers to a single piece of cloth without the characteristics of being divided by seams or cut into sections.
Nowadays, there are those who have śrāmaṇeras wear the five- or seven-strip robes of a bhikṣu; this is truly contrary to the Dharma.
Therefore, the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Tang dynasty, having witnessed it with his own eyes in the West, translated the *Ekottarakarma* (The Hundred and One Karmas), stating:

As for those who are śrāmaṇeras, their proper attire consists of the *man-tiao* (the single-layered robe). To suddenly don the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*) is a grave transgression and an abuse of the precepts.
This custom has long been prevalent in the land of China, yet it constitutes an unrighteous practice; do not allow them to wear it.
Regarding the "upholding of the ten precepts" (*śīla*), "receiving" means obtaining the ten precepts from a teacher, internalizing and maintaining them without violation.
The ten precepts refer to those beginning from the abstention from killing up to the abstention from handling gold, silver, or precious objects.

Now, the *śīla* (precepts) are the keen blades that guard against wrongdoing and cease evil; the *vinaya* (discipline) is the model and method for adjudicating the gravity of offenses, determining what is permitted or prohibited, and maintaining or violating the rules.
One is called a *śrāmaṇera* (novice monk) because by receiving these ten precepts, one obtains the name of a *śrāmaṇera*, thereby distinguishing oneself from others.
This is because their forms are identical. Regarding the initial foundation for entering the Way: it refers to leaving one's kin and severing attachments in the hope of seeking liberation.
Upon entering the Dharma-gate, one first receives the ten precepts as the foundation for the Way; only thereafter does one receive the Bhikṣu and Bodhisattva major precepts.
This is like constructing a multi-storied pavilion where the foundation is laid first. Thus, the *Mahā-upāya-sūtra* says: "It is like a person entering..."
The ocean: from the shallow to the deep. The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma is also like this; this is what that means.
When it says "foreign lands" (wàiguó) refers to those outside [China], namely the Hu regions of the north. The translators came from India (Tiānzhú), traveling through the Hu countries on their way;
thus they used the Hu language to translate into the language of China (Huáyán). The language of China refers to the speech of the Central Kingdom (Zhōnghuá) of this land.

Furthermore, "Śrāmaṇera" (Sī-tzŭ) means to cease and eliminate the evils of the seven branches of body and speech, extensively cultivate all manner of goodness, and compassionately rescue all living beings.
Now, "ceasing" (sī) pertains to self-benefit, while "compassion" (tzŭ) pertains to benefiting others. One who benefits both self and others is called a true son of the Buddha;
such a person does not fall into the practices of the partial or the Hinayana.
In the authentic Sanskrit of India, it is fully pronounced as *śramaṇera*. This translates into Chinese as "seeker of tranquility" (*qi-ji*).
"Tranquility" (*ji*) carries the meaning of "perfect stillness" (*yuan-ji*), which is another name for wondrous *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, one who has left the household life should seek to proceed toward that state of *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, it is also translated as "diligent man" (*qin-ce nan*).
"By diligently practicing with exertion, one eradicates all afflictions and proceeds to the shore of Nirvāṇa.

This verse provides a detailed explanation to clarify the correct meanings of both the Indian and Chinese terms, ensuring that the essential purport is purposeful and that the names and entities are without error.
These ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras fundamentally take the liberation from afflictions as their primary principle and the wondrous realization of nirvāṇa as their goal.

Thus it is said. The first three phrases correctly clarify the Sanskrit sounds; the subsequent nine phrases provide a general explanation of the Chinese terms. Regarding "Tianzhu" (India): [The remainder of the text follows.]
In ancient times it was called Shendu; sometimes it was called Xiandou; now it is called Indu. This is translated as "Moon.

This is because in that land, sages and worthies have followed one another’s tracks, guiding ordinary people and governing all things like the moon shining upon them; thus, many foreign nations commonly refer to it as the "Celestial Region" (Tianfang).
The territory is divided into five parts and has a circumference of over ninety thousand *li*. It borders the great ocean on three sides, and to the north...
It lies behind the Snowy Mountains, broad in the north and narrow in the south, shaped like a half-moon.
Its territory is divided into more than seventy kingdoms, all of which are called Tianzhu (India). Among them, the realm of Central India is the very center of the land of Jambudvīpa;
therefore, the Buddha was born therein. "Correct" (*zheng*) means not erroneous; it refers to the language of Tianzhu, which is the same as *Brahman* (Sanskrit).
The celestial sounds do not differ; this is truly because when the world was first formed, the assembly of Brahmā descended as the progenitors of humanity.
Having resided for generations in India (Tianzhu), their speech is the Sanskrit language and their script is the Sanskrit script.

Subsequently, as people followed their respective locations, the pronunciations each became different, yet it remains preserved only in India. To speak of it in its full form is to distinguish it from abbreviated versions.
Regarding the term "śrāmaṇera," it is formally rendered as *śramaṇera* using the Sanskrit language (*brahma-svara*). This is translated as "seeker of tranquility" (*qi ji*) and so forth.
This means that here in this land [China], one translates those words from the Western Heaven (India) into the language of the Central Kingdom.
"Seeking" (*qiu*) refers to aspiring for; it means that because he has originally received the ten precepts, he seeks transcendental *nirvāṇa*.
This is the Way. It does not seek the tainted, limited fruits of humans or devas. In Sanskrit it is called *nirvāṇa*; in the language of China, it is called "Perfect Quiescence" (*yuánjì*).

It is named "Perfect" (*yuán*) because the four virtues are fully complete; it is named "Quiescent" (*jì*) because the three obstacles are eternally severed. This differs from the Two Vehicles, which merely abandon the afflictions of views and thoughts and thus name their state "Liberation.

Therefore, it is said to be "Wondrous. Furthermore, these translations serve to bring out its specific meanings. Regarding the meaning: *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
Although there is a brief separation, one ultimately returns to *nirvāṇa*, for it is only when afflictions (*kleśa*) are completely extinguished that one realizes perfect quiescence (*parinirvāṇa*).
As for naming *nirvāṇa* the "shore," the shore is the "other shore" (*pāra*). This means that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is this shore, and afflictions are the middle current;
if afflictions are completely extinguished, one ascends to the other shore.
The Ten Precepts for Śrāmaṇeras: I shall now explain them in sequence. Having heard them, practice as taught;
the essence of the noble precepts will naturally become perfect.

This verse indicates the characteristics of the essence of the precepts. The first two lines provide a general indication of the characteristics of the precepts; the third line clarifies the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).

The fourth phrase correctly sets forth the essence of the precepts (*śīla*). Regarding the "ten training rules" (*daśa-śikṣāpada*): this refers to these ten precepts, which are precisely the training rules that a *śrāmaṇera* should practice and learn.
The statement that they are "explained in sequence" indicates that they are not presented out of order or in reverse. "Having heard them, one practices as taught":

"hearing" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*), and "practicing" refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*). By mentioning the first and the last, the intermediate stage—the wisdom of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*)—is implied.

This is wisdom (*prajñā*). If one hears but does not practice, it is like hearing others speak of food; one cannot satisfy oneself. Thus, a sutra says: "Though one may recite a thousand words, if one does not practice, what benefit is there?
It is better to hear but once and diligently cultivate, thereby gaining benefit. Regarding "the essence of the noble precepts being spontaneously perfected":
this refers to the unconditioned precept-essence (*avijñapti-śīla-sarīra*), which can bring about the fruits of the three vehicles of holiness; therefore, by upholding it, its essence is perfected.

It enables one to reach the other shore; whereas that which destroys it is like a leaking bag, sinking in the midst of the stream. As for "non-action" (*anabhisaṃskāra*): by relying on the teacher, one receives the arousal [of the precepts].
If they are not aroused, that is the end of it; once aroused, they immediately perfect one's nature. Thus, nature and cultivation mutually accomplish one another.

One spontaneously carries out good and spontaneously ceases evil, without waiting for further effort; hence it is called "non-action. Below, the specific characteristics of the precepts are explained.
Throughout one's life, one must not kill humans or non-humans; nor should one give others poison, cause abortions, or dispatch someone to end a life.
Furthermore, if one should take the life of another by any various means, one incurs a grave offense and brings upon oneself the calamity of breaking the precepts.
These two verses admonish both the killer and the victim, and delineate the characteristics of the offense. The first line admonishes the person who kills;
the second and fourth lines clarify the object of the killing; the third line clarifies the instruments of killing; the fifth and sixth lines clarify the method of killing;
and the final two lines conclude with the determination of the offense. "To refrain from killing for as long as life lasts" means to never commit an act of killing throughout one's entire lifetime.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of killing. First, using internal form: this refers to striking another with one’s own body, hands, head, or feet, causing them to die.
Second, using external form: this refers to hurling objects such as tiles, wood, swords, spears, bows, arrows, copper, iron, lead, or tin from a distance at another person, causing them to die.
Third, using both internal and external form: this refers to grasping objects such as tiles, wood, swords, spears, bows, arrows, copper, or iron with one’s hand [and then using them].
They beat him until he dies. If one does not kill using internal form, external form, or both internal and external form, it is by means of poison.
Furthermore, there are those who create pits, traps, snares, or nets; or who use incantations and spells; or who push others into water or fire to cause death.
All these belong to the category of those who may be killed. This includes both humans and non-humans. "Humans" refers to men, women, eunuchs, and so forth;
"non-humans" refers to ghosts, spirits, animals, insects, crawling creatures, and all things that possess life—these are all objects that may be killed.
To cause death by administering poison to another or inducing an abortion refers to the initial formation of a body within the womb.

Regarding the two life-faculties (*jīvitendriya*): if one employs the means to kill within them—such as giving poison to that woman, pressing upon her abdomen, causing her to perform heavy labor, making her carry heavy loads, making her run swiftly, or piercing her blood vessels;

or if, for the purpose of killing the mother, one intentionally causes an abortion—if the mother dies, one commits an inexpiable offense (*ānantarya-karma*); if the fetus dies, one commits a transgression (*pāyattika*).

[This constitutes] a transgression. If, for the purpose of killing the fetus, the fetus dies, one commits an irredeemable offense (*āpatti-pārājika*); if the mother dies, one commits a redeemable offense (*āpatti-duṣkṛta*).

Furthermore, if one cuts off another's life by various means—that is, employing various methods to cause them to lose their life—such as setting traps or pits, or sending them onto a path infested with wild beasts or bandits, or praising [such actions]...

To revile, scold, and abuse [another] so as to cause them to take their own life: "life" refers to the life-span (*āyus*), which is the continuous succession of the six sense faculties and the six consciousnesses;
this is called the life-span. When this succession is severed, it is termed death; hence, it is said that one "cuts off life. Regarding the phrase "one immediately incurs a grave offense":
if a person dies after committing a grave offense, it is irredeemable; if one harms another but they do not die, one commits a middling offense.

It is a transgression that may be confessed. If a non-human being dies, one commits a minor offense that may be confessed. However, if a Bodhisattva kills a non-human being, they commit an offense that cannot be confessed.
One who incurs the calamity of breaking the precepts violates the prohibitions of the Tathāgata;
in life, they shall not dwell together with the pure assembly, and after death, they will enter the Avīci Hell. Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi Sūtra* states: "The sin of killing can..."
It causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, a short lifespan;
second, much illness. Because they return their past lives to others life after life, it is called the calamity of breaking the precepts.
Nor should one, with a mind of anger, strike or cast down any sentient being; since the four great elements are all one and the same, how could one give rise to a harmful intent?
This verse awakens one to the fundamental nature as free from killing. The first two lines and the fourth line concern freedom from killing, while the third line concerns awakening.
Fundamentally, because one realizes the identity of all things, one is free from killing. Furthermore, there is no one who strikes or hurls objects at sentient beings with a mind of anger;
it is through anger that one commits killing. Anger belongs to the cause of killing, while striking and hurling are the conditions for killing.
"All sentient beings" refers to all living beings within the three realms and six paths of existence;
they all possess mind and consciousness, and are not like insentient objects such as wood or stone. Regarding the "four elements being identical":

all sentient beings form their bodies through the combination of earth, water, fire, and wind, and thus there is no difference between self and others. Therefore, the *Śrāmaṇerikā-śīla-sūtra* says: "Have compassion for all..."
Sentient beings are like one's own marrow; they are like one's father and mother, like one's child and one's own body—equal and without distinction.

With universal equanimity and a single mind, one should always be intent upon the Mahāyāna. How could one ever give rise to thoughts of harm? Since the four great elements are the same for all, [how can there be such a thing as killing?]
To kill another is to kill oneself; to be angry with others is to be angry with oneself. If one realizes that all phenomena are identical to oneself, then such things will not occur.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "If sentient beings habitually associate with anger, because the retribution for this has ripened, they fall into hell.
Upon emerging from hell, they receive the bodies of animals—tigers, wolves, lions, bears, and brown bears."
The wildcat and the weasel; the hawk and the falcon and their like—if they were to obtain a human body, they would possess the twelve evil codes of conduct (*duḥśīla*);
if they were to leave the household life, they would violate the precept against killing. One must be cautious regarding this.
"Do not instruct others to act; seeing them act, do not give rise to joy. One should simply arouse a mind of loving-kindness and bestow grace so that they may be at peace.
This verse precisely clarifies the two karmas of speech and mind: instructing others belongs to speech, while giving rise to joy belongs to the mind. Although one does not [act oneself...]
One may give instructions to others; however, when seeing others act, one must not give rise to joy in one's heart.

Since the offenses incurred by actions of body, speech, and mind have no fixed weight, one should instead give rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to bestow grace and bring about peace and happiness.
For while compassion (*karuṇā*) can extract suffering, loving-kindness can grant happiness. A renunciant son of the Śākya should not only refrain from committing acts of killing, but furthermore...

One practices the giving of loving-kindness and happiness. One takes pity on those who commit killing, for their transgressions will cause them to fall into the three miserable realms; one pities those who are killed, for they have no ground for refuge from their suffering.
"Beneficence" refers to bestowing grace, which consists of providing relief through both material wealth and the Dharma. This is done by means of a compassionate mind.
When the three spheres are empty and quiescent, one practices giving all day long without the notion of a giver, nor does one harbor any thought of expecting a reward.
The merit thus obtained is like space; it is beyond the reach of thought or calculation.
"All sentient beings without exception are future Buddhas; one should always arouse reverence and mindfulness so that they may attain liberation early.
This verse accords with the truth and engenders respect. The first two lines concern that which is revered; the latter two lines concern that which is capable of revering. (1)
"All sentient beings" refers to all those within the six realms and four modes of birth.

Although they inherently possess the wisdom and consciousness of the Tathāgata, they are shrouded by various forms of ignorance and afflictions; thus, they are called "sentient beings. Therefore, a sutra says:
"All sentient beings are fully endowed with the pure virtues and marks of the Tathāgata, yet because of their delusive thoughts, they do not realize them. This is so.
"Furthermore, those who are all future Buddhas possess the pure marks and characteristics of a Tathāgata;

thus we know that sentient beings have been fundamentally enlightened from the beginning and do not need to become Buddhas again. Yet they are called 'future' because they still harbor illusory delusions."
This is spoken merely from the perspective of conventional traces. For one who has realized the principle, it is not so.

That one should always give rise to a heart of reverence and admiration is because [the sentient being] inherently possesses the marks and attributes of virtue; therefore, one must constantly cultivate a mind of reverence and admiration. To instead harbor thoughts of harm is to kill the Buddhas of the future.
As for the thought of causing them to attain liberation early, this refers to all sentient beings, even though they possess...
Regarding these marks of virtue, because they are considered by him to be the delusions of various afflictions (*kleśa*) and thus not yet realized, he gives rise to thoughts of compassion,
vowing that others may swiftly be liberated from affliction and ascend to perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"I vow that from the time I attain Buddhahood, there shall be no one in my land who kills; may all cultivate the path of the One Vehicle and together ascend to the fruit of eternal quiescence.

This verse expresses the dedication of merit through the making of vows. Of the preceding five verses, the former belong to the category of functional efficacy, while this verse belongs to the category of the fruit of the precepts.
One experiences the sublime retribution of the environment and its inhabitants; yet, the act of making a vow inherently includes dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
By means of this vow, one dedicates the roots of goodness cultivated by oneself toward three objects: the true nature (*dharmatā*), enlightenment (*bodhi*), and sentient beings.

The first phrase constitutes the dedication of oneself toward the true nature and enlightenment, while the following three phrases constitute the dedication of [merit] to sentient beings, directing them toward the true nature and enlightenment.
"Ti" (Dhīḥ). True reality (*tathatā*) is suchness; bodhi is the Buddha-way. The vow "when I myself attain Buddhahood" clarifies that one does not seek the path of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
"Time" refers to the moment when practice is fulfilled and the fruit perfected, and one realizes equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

In that land, there shall be no one who kills. This refers to the world where he will attain Buddhahood in the future. All sentient beings therein practice loving-kindness and possess no thoughts of anger or harm;
they all cultivate the path of the One Vehicle. This means that the sentient beings of that land cultivate only the Buddha-vehicle and do not practice the paths of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
They all ascend together to the fruit of eternal quiescence. "Eternal" (chang) means unchanging; that is to say—

It is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Because the Dharma-body is fundamentally free from arising and ceasing, it is called "quiescent" (*śānta*). It is that which is realized through the fruit of supreme wondrous enlightenment.
By personally upholding the precepts and refraining from all evil, one accomplishes the Dharma-body, thereby bringing about a transformative influence upon the sentient beings within the land.
Both shall realize the fruit of eternal quiescence. Question: Why should one dedicate the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera toward the Buddha-way? Answer:

The essence of the ten śrāmaṇera precepts encompasses both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna; they are not intended for the Śrāvaka alone. If the mind is great, the precepts are expansive, and one achieves the perfection of Right Enlightenment.
If the mind is inferior, the precepts are limited, and one personally attains the four fruits [of the śramaṇa]. It is like having no transcendence [if one lacks the aspiration for the Great Way].
Even if one observes many precepts with such a mind, the resulting merit and retribution will merely lead to rebirth among humans or devas.

According to the *Śrāmaṇerikā-śīla-sūtra*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, and other texts, one should seek the Mahāyāna and dedicate [the merit] toward the Buddha-way. Furthermore, on the days a Bodhisattva observes the fast, they receive and uphold the ten precepts;
the first five precepts are identical to those of a śrāmaṇera, while the latter five are distinct. Thus, we know that one must dedicate [the merit] toward the Mahāyāna.
This is not a matter of mere conjecture, but rather the true purport of all the sūtras. Furthermore, the precepts are like level ground from which all myriad virtues arise;
if one plants exceptional causes, one will surely obtain great fruits. The explanation of the first precept is concluded.
One must not steal the property of others—be it gold, silver, plants, wood, or even the possessions of birds and beasts—and must never take them by private theft.
Whether by deception, fraud, or seizure; whether evading taxes or stealing at passes and ferries;
whether acting on one's own behalf or instructing another to do so—all such acts violate the prohibitions of a śrāmaṇera.

This verse clarifies the thief, the object stolen, and the characteristics of the offense incurred through the three types of action (*karma*). The first line provides a general indication of the agent and the object;
the agent of theft refers to the person, while the object stolen refers to the thing. The second and third lines specifically identify the objects stolen.
The fourth, fifth, and sixth lines describe the methods of theft. The seventh line clarifies the actions of body and speech, while also encompassing the mental action (*manas-karma*), because...
At the moment one resolves to steal, it belongs to the mental karma (*manas-karman*). The eighth phrase establishes the offense. Regarding "one must not steal another's property":
when an object belongs to another and is guarded by that other person, to take it without being given is called stealing. "Wealth" (*dhana*) is a general term for objects;
gold, silver, grass, wood, and so forth—meaning that among objects, there is nothing more valuable than gold and silver. The seven [precious substances]... [text ends].
Regarding "jewels" and so forth: among objects, nothing is lighter than a single blade of grass, a single tree, a single needle, or a single thread.

As for "objects belonging to birds and beasts," this refers to things consumed or guarded by birds and beasts. The phrase "even unto" indicates that the preceding and succeeding terms encompass those in between.
Although gold, silver, and so forth were mentioned previously, their specific ownership had not yet been distinguished; the intention here is now to...
Regarding superior things, these are the property of the Three Jewels, the preceptors, and one’s parents; regarding middling things, these are the property of the state and the people;

and regarding inferior things, these extend down to the property of ghosts, spirits, birds, and beasts. One must not privately or secretly take any of them. "Privately stealing" is called *qiè* (to pilfer).
This means that for the aforementioned items, one must not only refrain from theft, but also must not privately or secretly take them. (*Weishi lun*)
The *Juedun* (Decisive Discourse) states: "To secretly take up and read the sutras and śāstras of others, even down to a single phrase, constitutes the offense of stealing textual passages.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states: "If one steals another's secret formulas, one commits a grave offense. Regarding the terms used: "to deceive" (*qi*) means to defraud;

"to overreach" (*ling*) means to insult or treat with contempt; "to feign" (*zha*) means to act with guile and deceit; "to falsely assume another's name" (*wei cheng ta ming*) means to misrepresent oneself by using another's identity; and "to seize by force" (*duo qiang*) refers to taking by means of compulsion.
"Taking" means that one must not only refrain from stealing, but also from deceiving, defrauding, or seizing by force.
Regarding "stealing taxes or evading customs posts": "taxes" refers to goods that ought to be taxed; one must not conceal them or attempt to pass through customs posts or ferries in secret.
This indicates that one must not only refrain from seizing through fraud, but also from evading taxes.

Crossing a ferry: if it concerns property belonging to the Three Jewels or one’s parents, and one explains the Dharma and exhorts them so that the authorities do not take the toll, there is no offense.
In this context, the gravity of the object is determined by its value in money to establish the offense.

Whether one acts oneself or instructs another, acting oneself pertains to the body, while instructing another pertains to speech; both offenses are equal. "All who violate the prohibitions of a śrāmaṇera" refers to those mentioned above.
Regarding property: whether by theft, fraud, or smuggling across a border—whether committed by oneself or incited in another—one incurs the offense of stealing.

Among these, the characteristics of the transgression are as follows: if, with a thieving mind, one takes another's five coins or an object worth five coins, and moves it from its location to another place, one commits an offense of irreparable retribution (*pārājika*).
However, if remorse arises in the mind and one returns the item to its original place, [the offense is not established].

If one commits an act that is not to be repented (anāpatti), yet while lifting or moving an object, it has not yet left its original place, one commits a transgression that is to be repented (sāvadya).

If one conceives the intention to steal but does not yet take it, one commits a minor transgression that is to be repented. If one takes it but the value is less than five coins, one commits a middling transgression that is to be repented.
This applies if one perceives the object as one's own property, or perceives the owner as a consenting friend, or perceives it as being for temporary use, or believes there is no owner.
[This applies to] thoughts. If the mind is deranged and one is not self-aware, thinking "I am a śrāmaṇera," there is no offense in any case. The Sūtra says:
"The sin of stealing can cause sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms.
If they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, poverty; second, having no mastery over shared wealth, and constantly being [born as] slaves or animals."
Repaying past debts to others,
one should practice noble yielding upon leaving the household life; keeping the mind fixed on the six points of harmonious respect, one should not take what is not rightfully one's own,
but always keep in mind the practice of giving.
This verse clarifies the practice of giving through harmonious conduct. Regarding "one who has left the household life should practice yielding": to place others before oneself is called yielding;

furthermore, it means to be humble and not presume upon one's own worth. If even laypeople regard wealth lightly and value righteousness, how much more so for a son of the Śākya, who originally renounced fame and profit to leave the household life for the sake of the Way, viewing gold and silk as if they were great venomous snakes—how could he possibly [cling to them]?

Is it not the case that one who yields in an unrighteous manner lacks such [virtue]? One whose mind dwells upon the six aspects of harmony and respect (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*) possesses these harmonies in two senses.

First is harmony of principle (*dharma-sāmagrī*), which means that they equally realize cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Second is harmony of practice (*vastu-sāmagrī*), which has six aspects: first, harmony of precepts (*śīla-sāmagrī*), meaning they cultivate them together;

second, harmony of view (*dṛṣṭi-sāmagrī*), meaning they understand together; third, harmony of body (*kāya-sāmagrī*), meaning they dwell together; fourth, harmony of material goods (*lābha-sāmagrī*), meaning they share them equally; fifth, harmony of speech (*vāk-sāmagrī*), meaning there is no contention; and sixth, harmony of mind (*manas-sāmagrī*).
They share the same joy. Therefore, it is said that without the true mind, one cannot possess the six dharmas; without the six dharmas, one cannot harmonize the multitude.
If the multitude is not in harmony, it is contrary to the Way of reverence and compliance. If the mind lacks righteousness and yielding, these six harmonies will be lost.
As for "not taking what is not rightfully one's own while constantly mindful of practicing giving," because the mind harbors righteousness and yielding, one does not take.
It is not material wealth; it is obtained according to one's giving. One enjoys it with contentment, remains mindful of the suffering of sentient beings, and passes it on to them.
Therefore, it is said: "Constantly mindfully practice the giving of alms."
May I attain the path of perfect enlightenment; may there be no thieves within my land; may all practice purely the perfection of generosity, adorning themselves with both merit and wisdom.
This verse expresses a vow of dedication, seeking the sublime retribution of both the environment and its inhabitants. Indeed, one should cultivate all virtuous deeds.
If one does not make vows and dedicate merit toward unsurpassed bodhi, one will ultimately achieve only the tainted, minor fruits of the realms of humans and devas.

If the mind does not abandon theft, by what means could one become a Buddha in a land where sentient beings do not steal? If one does not practice the giving of wisdom, there is no cause for perfect enlightenment;
how then could one inspire sentient beings in the Buddha-land to all practice the *dāna-pāramitā*? It is because...

By practicing generosity, maintaining ethical discipline, and cultivating right contemplation, one attains rebirth as a sentient being within the Buddha-land whose body is adorned with the two kinds of provisions:
merit and wisdom. This concludes the second section on ethical discipline.
Lustful desire is a base and evil matter; a śrāmaṇera must not engage in it. To violate [this rule] with a human male or female, or with an animal, one immediately incurs a grave offense.

This verse rebukes desire and establishes the offense by identifying the agent who commits it, the object committed against, and the resulting transgression. The first line rebukes the impurity of desire; the second line...
The first phrase indicates the person who commits the offense; the second and third phrases clarify the object of the offense;
and the fourth phrase establishes the transgression. "Lustful desire" refers to the union of two bodies. "Vile and evil" refers to lewd and unwholesome conduct.

A śrāmaṇera must not engage in such acts, for they are both base and improper for one who follows the pure practice of renunciation. Moreover, among the roots of birth and death, lust is the foremost.
A śrāmaṇera leaves the secular world fundamentally with the aim of transcending the three realms and emerging from the mire of desire;
how could he again bind himself to the causes of outflows and fall forever into the depths of saṃsāra? Regarding "men, women, and animals": "men" refers to human males and non-human males;
"women" refers to human females and non-human females. "Non-humans" include devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and even eunuchs.
Regarding the "two organs" and so forth: "animals" refers to all birds and beasts. "Those capable of being objects of sexual desire" refers to those who, if violated, incur a grave offense.
This means that if one commits an act of impurity with the aforementioned humans, women, men, or animals, one incurs an unforgivable offense (*āpatti-ānantarya*).

Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: if one engages in sexual intercourse with a woman at the three locations—the anus, the urinary tract, or the mouth—one commits an offense entailing irreparable transgression (anantarya).
If one engages in sexual intercourse with a man at the two locations—the anus or the mouth—one commits an offense entailing irreparable transgression.

If two bodies come together but cease before sexual intercourse occurs, it is an offense of the middle grade that may be confessed. If one has formed the intention to act but the bodies have not yet come together, it is an offense of the minor grade that may be confessed.
With the exception of the three [sensitive] locations, if one engages in sexual intercourse with other parts of the body, it is an offense of the middle grade that may be confessed.
If a śrāmaṇera is violated by another and experiences pleasure in his own mind, it is an offense that cannot be confessed; if he does not experience such pleasure in his mind, it is not an offense.
If one experiences pleasure while committing an offense that requires confession (*sappatikamma-āpatti*), it is like obtaining food when hungry or obtaining a drink when thirsty.
If one does not experience pleasure, it is like hot iron entering the body or being pierced by a blade. Furthermore, one must not intentionally play with the hand to cause the emission of impurity.
As the Blessed One said: "I have two bodies: first, the physical body (*jāti-kāya*); second, the body of precepts (*sīla-kāya*). If a person...
If someone were to damage a stupa made of the seven precious gems erected over my physical body, reaching as high as the Brahma Heaven, their transgression could still be repented.
However, to damage my body of precepts is a transgression of immeasurable magnitude, resulting in retribution like that of the Naga King Elapatra.
The *Nirvana Sutra* states: "If sentient beings habitually associate with greed and desire, because this retribution ripens, they fall into hell. From the earth...
Upon emerging from hell, one receives the body of an animal—such as a pigeon, a sparrow, a mandarin duck, a fish, a turtle, a monkey, a deer, or their like.

If one should obtain a human birth, one receives the body of a eunuch, a woman, a hermaphrodite, one without sexual organs, or a prostitute. Even if one manages to leave the household life, [one remains subject to such conditions].
Having violated the precept against sexual misconduct,
one should eliminate thoughts of greed and desire; close the gates of the six sense faculties, contemplate the body as the root of suffering,
and set one's will upon the path of purity.
This verse teaches the purification of body and mind to cultivate contemplative wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "eliminating thoughts of desire and closing the six sense faculties," it means that not only does the body refrain from sexual misconduct, but the mind likewise does not give rise to such thoughts; one seeks to ensure they do not arise.
Contemplate this: one must close the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Once the six faculties are restrained, contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*) will be accomplished.

Regarding the term "passion" (*qing*), it carries the meaning of craving and attachment. This refers to the six sense-faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—craving and attaching to the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*):
forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena. Therefore, the *Śrāmaṇerikā-śīla-sūtra* states: "The eyes do not gaze lustfully; the ears do not listen lustfully."
The nose does not lust after fragrances; the mouth does not utter lewd words; the mind harbors no desire. One contemplates the four great elements of the body as fundamentally non-existent.
Calculating earth, water, fire, and air, one finds there is no person and no self, no life-span and no soul. What is there to lust after? What is there to be attached to?
To contemplate the body as the root of suffering means to realize the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and the pain of separation from what one loves.

There is suffering: the suffering of association with what is disliked, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, the suffering of various calamities great and small, and the arising of the four hundred and four diseases due to the imbalance of the four elements.
Furthermore, internally, one is afflicted by anger, sorrow, doubt, regret, sensual desire, and so forth.
Externally, one is afflicted by cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, thirst, and the like.
All such sufferings arise because, due to that initial moment of inverted thought and a lustful mind, one entered the mother’s womb and formed this body.
Thus, this body is the root of ten thousand entanglements and the source of all suffering. If there were not that initial thought of inversion, how [could this have come to be]?
Because there is this body of manifold suffering, one knows that this body exists entirely due to lustful desire.

To cease all suffering, one must eliminate thoughts of desire and cultivate contemplative wisdom—namely, contemplating the impurity of the body, the suffering of sensation, the impermanence of the mind, and the non-self of phenomena.
When samādhi manifests before one, one then realizes the unborn; and thus, the multitude...

When suffering is extinguished along with its accompaniments, all worldly entanglements are cast aside. For one whose will is set upon the path of purity—that is, the path of detachment from desire—one attains *nirvāṇa* upon such detachment;
hence it is said that "the exhaustion of craving is *nirvāṇa*. When a *śrāmaṇera* leaves the household life, his will is directed toward seeking *nirvāṇa*.
If craving were not exhausted, how could he be called by the name "Seeker of Quiescence" (*śamaṇa*)?
"May my buddha-field, when I attain Buddhahood, have no one who violates the precepts; may all cultivate pure brahma-conduct, and the three virtues [of body, speech, and mind] be perfectly luminous.

This verse expresses a vow of dedication, seeking the attainment of the two sublime retributions: the primary (the Buddha-body) and the secondary (the buddha-field). "Attaining Buddhahood" refers to the primary retribution.

"Superiority of retribution" refers to the fact that in this land there is no violation of prohibitions, up to and including the attainment of perfect clarity. This is the superiority of the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment). "Prohibitions" (*jin*) refers to the restraints;
it means the precepts established by the Tathāgata, which one is not permitted to transgress. "Brahmacarya" (*fanxing*) refers to pure conduct.
To ensure that both the phrasing and the meaning are clearly understood, the term is expressed in both Chinese and Sanskrit as "pure *brahmacarya*. This is because one's own precepts are pure.

Therefore, sentient beings who practice the Brahma-conduct are inspired to be born in that land. Because they have eliminated desire and thought, the sentient beings of that land possess the perfect clarity of the three virtues.

These three virtues are the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and liberation (*vimukti*). They are called "three" [in number], while "permanence, bliss, self, and purity" are called their "virtues.
Like the character for "one" (一) in the world, they are neither sequential nor distinct, neither merged nor deficient; they are luminously pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
Its essence pervades the ten directions; therefore, it is called "perfectly luminous. Because one upholds the precepts, the Dharma-body is pure.
Because lustful thoughts have been eliminated, the wisdom of Prajñā is radiant. Because the holy life has been established, one is liberated from birth-and-death and afflictions.
The third precept is concluded.
A *śrāmaṇera* should not engage in false or deceptive speech; claiming to have attained what has not been attained, or falsely asserting realization of the profound and sublime Dharma;
using flowery, ornate, or frivolous words; or engaging in double-tongued speech to sow discord among others.
"Speaking ill and reviling; / Slandering one another"—this verse clarifies the four branches of the offense of verbal karma.
Regarding "false speech and deceptive words": it is to say one has seen what one has not seen.

To say one has seen what one has not seen, to say one has heard what one has not heard, or to say one has heard what one has not heard—when speech contradicts the mind, it is called false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).
To speak what is not true, to deceive the ignorant, and to delude others, is called deception (*śāṭhya*). To diligently urge others to do what should not be done is to speak what is not true;
it is not the conduct of one who has left the household life. To claim what one has not attained...
Regarding the statement "to falsely claim to have realized the profound and subtle Dharma": "falsely" (*miao*) means deceptive or erroneous; "realized" (*zheng*) means to have attained awakening.

This "profound and subtle Dharma" is also called the "Dharma of the Superior Person" (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*). The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "I have, in various ways, rebuked false speech and praised the absence of false speech.
Even in jest, one should not speak falsely, let alone intentionally speaking falsehoods. [He who] says of himself: "I..."
If one claims to have attained the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), up to the fruit of an arhat; or claims to have attained dhyāna, samādhi, or the meditative absorption of *samāpatti*;
or claims that devas, nāgas, or spirits have come to one’s presence to inquire about the Dharma and to make offerings to one—this constitutes an offense of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
Regarding the characteristics of this offense: if one says to another person, "I have attained the Way," one commits an offense of immediate retribution.
If one resolves to speak falsely but has not yet spoken, one commits an offense that is a minor transgression requiring confession (*duṣkṛta*).

Even when words have been uttered, if the person addressed does not understand them, one commits a middling transgression requiring confession. If one speaks but does not fully express one's intent, one likewise commits a middling transgression requiring confession.

If one says, "I do not fall into the three miserable realms," one commits a middling transgression requiring confession. If one says, "I maintain the precepts purely; lust does not [afflict me]," [one likewise commits a middling transgression requiring confession].

Rising. Regarding that which is unreal: it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika). If, for the sake of fame or gain, one acts with composure while sitting, rising, walking, standing, or speaking, manifesting the appearance of having attained the Path in order to make others believe so, it is an offense of expiation.

Furthermore, if one does not recite the sūtras but claims to recite them; if one is not a master of Abhidharma but claims to be a master of Abhidharma; if one is not a master of Vinaya but claims to be a master of Vinaya; if one does not sit... [and so forth].
To say one is practicing meditation when one is not; to say one has practiced recitation when one has not; all such instances constitute an offense requiring confession (*pratikarmanīya*).
Likewise, to say one has heard what was not heard, to say one has seen what was not seen, or to claim something exists when it does not—all these constitute offenses requiring confession.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There are two kinds of thieves in the world: first, those who are not of pure conduct yet claim for themselves to be of pure conduct; second,"

For the sake of food and drink, one speaks untruths that are not real and do not belong to oneself; thus, before others, one intentionally utters false speech, claiming, "I have attained the state of a superior person.
Among these, one who acts for the sake of food and drink is the greatest thief, because they steal the food and drink offered by others.
It would be better to eat ashes and charcoal, to swallow excrement and soil, or to have one's belly ripped open with a sharp blade, than to act with such falsehood.
They claim to have attained the qualities of a superior person (*uttamapudgala*) and thereby receive offerings. The *Dhyānaguhyārtha-sūtra* states:

"If one has not actually realized the contemplation of white bones and so forth, yet claims, 'I have attained the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*)', this person, after the end of their life, will fall into the Avīci Hell as swiftly as a flash of lightning or falling rain, for a lifespan of one kalpa.
Upon emerging from that hell, they will fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*) for eight thousand [kalpas]."
Year after year, they swallow glowing iron balls. Emerging from the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), they fall among the animals (*tiryagyoni*).

There, they are born to constantly carry heavy burdens; upon death, their skins are flayed again. This continues for five hundred lifetimes. When they are finally reborn among humans, they suffer from deafness, blindness, muteness, and lameness, with a hundred ailments serving as their clothing.
Such various sufferings cannot be fully described. Furthermore, the verse on the primary retribution (*vipāka*) states: "Deceiving through false speech..."
Human ingenuity is clever; suffering in hell is clumsy. Flaming saws split their bodies; hot iron plows their tongues.
Molten copper is poured over them; they are ground by hard steel. Their grief shatters their marrow; their moans are constant and choked.

The Verse on the Ripening of Karma says: "Lying leads one into the three miserable realms. Once the retribution for those sins is settled, residual karma causes rebirth in the human realm, yet one remains..."
Slander brings constant anxiety and bondage; one will, in turn, be deceived by others. A heart of resentment burns like fire. The wise do not blame others;
they verify the fruit and must extinguish its cause. Regarding "ornate and frivolous speech": *qi* (綺) refers to brocade; *mi* (靡) means beautiful.
This refers to flowery speech that adorns and beautifies, like weaving fine silk brocade to delude the human mind. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Though words may be true, if they are spoken at an inappropriate time, they also fall under frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*). The *Fayuan zhulin* states:
"Loyal words are used to manifest principle, while flowery speech causes one to deviate from truth. Because of loyalty, there is reality; because there is reality..."
Therefore, virtue arises. Because virtue arises, one becomes a sage. Due to frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*), falsehood arises.

Because of falsehood, transgression arises. Because transgression arises, one undergoes suffering. Thus, one should know that those who seek the principle and aspire to sagehood must speak truthfully.
If speech is false, it ultimately deviates from the principle. If words are not correct, they are all termed frivolous speech. Furthermore, as for various forms of frivolous speech...
It only increases self-indulgence for oneself and others, fosters all manner of unwholesome states, and leads to falling into the three miserable realms.

Even when one later emerges as a human, people will not believe any correct speech one utters. As a verse in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* says: "There are those who fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), with flames of fire issuing from their mouths;
they cry out in all four directions—this is the fault of verbal karma. If one desires a wide reputation, [one must guard against such faults].
It is that which people trust and accept; therefore, one should be sincere and must not engage in frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*). The verse on the direct retribution states:

"Frivolous speech lacks meaning and principle, causing the human mind to become deluded and confused. It destroys one's own roots of goodness, resulting in molten copper being poured into one's split-open mouth."
Flaming iron burns their tongues; their internal organs are all scorched and rotten. This agony is unbearable; they wail and cry out in constant lamentation.
As the *Gāthā on the Retribution of Habituation* says: "Idle words obscure the True Principle; because of this, one sinks into the evil realms.

When departing from that state to return as a human, one’s speech lacks clarity and understanding. Born without a mind of faith, one is forever an object of others' ridicule. May [beings] be awakened by this.
How shameful! Why not cite the scriptural passages? Regarding "double-tongued speech that causes division":

this refers to conveying words from one party to another to incite strife and discord, thereby causing fathers and sons, brothers, and friends to alienate themselves from their bonds of affection and righteousness;

even to the point of praising someone in one's presence and slandering them behind their back, or being agreeable to their face while being contrary behind their back. As the Buddha said in a verse in the *Huashou jing* (Śrīmālā-sūtra): "Speaking with evil words..."
Divisive speech; delighting in exposing the faults of others—such unwholesome persons commit every kind of evil. The verse on the primary retribution says:
"Those who use divisive speech to sow discord among people shall be torn asunder in hell. The wardens of hell will split their mouths, and flaming knives will cut their tongues.
When such is the nature of their suffering, they are further afflicted by hunger and thirst. Bound by their own evil karma, they have no freedom. Return...

They drink the blood within one's body. The verse on the ripening of karmic retribution says: "Slander and defamation harm others deeply; one will surely undergo the sufferings of the three miserable realms.
Even if one should obtain a human body, the remaining retribution will still persist: one's kin and retinue will be mostly wicked and evil, acting in opposition and indulging in unrestrained anger."
However, one does not forget those evils. In the hells, there is neither past nor present. To speak with harsh words and to revile is defined as "abusive speech" (*pāruṣya*);
to address someone directly is called "reviling," while to extend it to others is called "abusing. Harsh speech refers to uttering coarse and wicked words, such as insults, slanders, and curses.
The *Dharmapada-sūtra* states: "Though one may be a śramaṇa, if one does not restrain body and speech, speaking coarse words and evil talk, [one will suffer] much..."

Slanderous speech leads to the departure of the soul upon physical death, causing one to transmigrate through the three miserable realms, undergoing birth and death by oneself and enduring immeasurable suffering.
It is that which the Buddhas and noble sages do not cherish. Even if one’s body is free of fault, if one is not careful regarding the karma of speech, one will likewise fall into the evil paths.
A verse from the *Karmavipāka-sūtra* says: "Harsh words provoke and distress others; one delights in exposing the private secrets of others; [and being] stubborn and fierce..."
Difficult to subdue, one is reborn as a *jvalamukha* (flame-mouthed) hungry ghost. The *Āgama* Sūtra says:
"It would be better to cut out one's tongue with a sharp sword than to fall into the three evil realms through evil speech and coarse words. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are two kinds of people who will invariably enter hell: those who do not lead a pure life (*brahmacarya*) yet claim to lead a pure life, and those who truly lead a pure life yet [deny it]."
They slandered him by claiming he did not practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Even if it were true, one should not speak such things.
The Buddha said in the *Mahāvaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*: "Know that even the karma of slandering a single four-line verse will certainly lead to rebirth in hell."
They shall never behold a Buddha. Because they looked upon those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta with evil eyes, they receive the retribution of being eyeless.
Because they slandered those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta with evil speech, they receive the retribution of being tongueless.
In the *Bodhicittotpāda-viśuddhi-sūtra*, the Buddha addressed sixty bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds, saying: "In the past, under the teaching of Krakucchanda Buddha, you..."
Having left the household life to study the Path, you were entirely negligent regarding the precepts, extensive learning, and the merits of the dhūta practices.
At that time, there were two Dharma-preaching bhikṣus whom you slandered for their celibacy;

for the sake of gain and fame, you harbored jealousy and greed toward the families of those teachers who were your own kinsmen and patrons, as well as toward the relatives of those two Dharma-preaching masters.
O friend, donor, you further cause division and dissension; through double-tongued speech and insults, you sow doubt and prevent the arising of faith.
By speaking what is not the Dharma, you cause those who possess reverence and faith to sever their roots of goodness and create all manner of obstacles.
Because of this karma, you shall fall into the Avīci Great Hell for sixty-two hundred thousand years;
furthermore, you shall fall into the Saṃjīva Hell for forty thousand years; and furthermore, for twenty thousand years.
They fall into the Black Rope Hell (*Kālasūtra-naraka*). Furthermore, for eight hundred thousand years, they fall into the Hot Hell (*Tapana-naraka*).
After their life has ended in that hell, they later obtain a human body; however, due to the obstruction of their karma, they are born blind and sightless for five hundred lifetimes.
In whatever place they are born, they will all be dull-witted and forget their original nature; their roots of goodness will be blocked, their power diminished, and they will be abandoned by all.
They will constantly be bullied, loathed, reviled, and slandered by others;
they will always be born in borderlands, in places of poverty and lowliness, or into families of inferior lineage. After casting off this body, for the subsequent five hundred [years]...
During the year when the True Dharma is extinguished, they will again be reborn in evil lands and evil places, into families of low birth, poverty, and meanness.

They will constantly be subjected to slander, lose their original resolve, and face perpetual obstacles to the roots of goodness they have cultivated. Although they may briefly encounter the light of wisdom, [they shall not abide in it].
One remains shrouded in obscuration; only after those five hundred years have passed will all karmic obstacles be utterly extinguished.

As stated in the sutras, one must be most diligent in exercising caution. To slander [the Dharma] with even a single word brings calamity for the duration of an aeon—how can one not stand in awe of this?

Regarding those who speak of right and wrong to one another: this refers to speaking of others behind their backs, or speaking of oneself to others, inciting strife and contention, even bearing witness to the crimes of others, or proclaiming the faults of others. As a verse in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* says:
"If a person utters even a single falsehood, that person will quickly be held in contempt; all virtuous people will abandon them, and even the gods will not protect them."
He constantly harbors hatred and jealousy toward others, commits evil against sentient beings, and employs skillful means to harass and disturb them;

because of this, he enters hell. The Vinaya states: "As a son of the Buddha, one’s speech should always be truthful. One should not take an oath to clear oneself or to demonstrate that others do not believe one.
Even if one is falsely slandered, one should still not make a vow. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus had a minor matter.
Upon arriving, he immediately uttered a curse, saying: "If I were to do such a thing, may I fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma.
If you were to do such a thing, you too shall fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma."
The Buddha said: "It should not be done so. It is permitted to speak these words: 'If I have committed such an act, I take refuge in the Buddha;
if you have committed such an act, you also take refuge in the Buddha. According to these four branches of vocal karma:

the first, the false claim of having realized holiness or attained the state of a superior person, constitutes an offense that cannot be rectified; the latter three and other minor instances of false speech do not."
Offenses can be repented. Thus, the *Adbhuta-dharma-paryāya Sūtra* states: The Buddha told Prince Jeta, "There are two kinds of false speech:
one is grave, and the other is light. For the sake of offerings, one outwardly manifests diligence while inwardly practicing perversity and turbidity;
one falsely claims to others that one has attained the state of dhyāna, or says that one has seen the Buddha, seen dragons, or seen ghosts. Such a person..."
This is called great false speech. One who commits this offense falls into the Avīci Hell. Furthermore, there is false speech that can cause the killing of people or the destruction of households;
there is also false speech that violates agreements and causes others to harbor resentment.

Such as these are called minor false speech, for which one falls into the minor hells. As for other instances of joking or matters concealed for the sake of propriety, they are restrained [from being classified as such].
Regarding matters, if one says something exists when it does not, or says something does not exist when it does, one does not violate the precepts.
The *Śrāmaṇerikā-śīla-sūtra* states: "Do not propagate evil upon seeing it; do not proclaim evil upon hearing it. Avoid harsh words and false analogies;

always practice the four immeasurables. Do not engage in improper speech; whenever you speak, speak of the Path. Constantly extol the sūtras and the Dharma. This is the right precept of a Bodhisattva: to set one's will upon the Mahāyāna and not [act otherwise]."
This is the Hīnayāna.
The worthy one maintains a single mind, remains far removed from the faults of verbal karma, and does not engage in deceitful conduct;
thus, his wholesome dharmas increase day by day.

This verse clarifies that the abandonment of evil and the increase of goodness constitute the function of the precepts. A worthy person who single-mindedly maintains [the precepts] remains far removed from the faults of verbal karma.
There are four such faults of verbal karma; they arise immediately upon encountering circumstances. If one is not single-minded, one will be unable to guard oneself;
how then could one avoid these faults? Therefore, a sutra says: "Guard the mouth as one would a jar; defend the mind as one would a city. This is so.
Furthermore, regarding "not practicing deception so that wholesome dharmas increase daily": this means that if one always speaks the truth, wholesome dharmas will naturally increase;
if one's conduct is not deceptive, then concentration and wisdom will grow day by day.
"Those who later attain the Unsurpassed Way, And all those who possess truthful speech, Shall come to be born in that land, Fully endowed with the four analytical knowledges.

This verse clarifies that because the cause is extraordinary, the fruit is supreme. By eliminating the four faults of speech, one attains the Unsurpassed Way and becomes fully endowed [with these qualities].

They possess the karmic retribution (*vipāka*) of the eight musical qualities and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); thus, their environmental retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*) is likewise so.

As for the four analytical knowledges: first, the analytical knowledge of rapidity; second, the analytical knowledge of vastness; third, the analytical knowledge of profundity; and fourth, the inexhaustible analytical knowledge.

They are also called the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), because the wisdom of all Bodhisattvas is clear and lucid, and their eloquent exposition is unimpeded; hence they are called "unhindered."
Eloquence (*pratibhāna*). First is the unimpeded eloquence regarding meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), which refers to penetrating all the principles and meanings of all phenomena without obstruction.
Second is the unimpeded eloquence regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), which refers to discerning the names and designations of all phenomena without obstruction.
Third is the unimpeded eloquence regarding expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), which refers to [speaking] in accordance with the diverse languages and customs of all sentient beings.
Fourth is the unimpeded eloquence of analytical exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

This refers to expounding the teachings in accordance with the inclinations and capacities of all sentient beings, such that the discourse flows without obstruction and each individual attains understanding.
Because it is free from falsehood and devoid of meaninglessness, it is perfectly harmonious and unimpeded.
Because he abandoned divisive speech, he attained the unimpeded eloquence that realizes the profound meaning of all phenomena.
Because he abandoned harsh and coarse speech, sentient beings experience happiness, and thus he attained the inexhaustible and unimpeded eloquence of joyful exposition.
Because he abandoned frivolous and useless speech, he attained [the eloquence] to expound...
To speak with swift eloquence and unimpeded辩 (discernment) concludes the explanation of the fourth precept.
One must not drink, taste, or smell various grains, flowers, fruits, or wine; nor should one give them to others, for this increases the karma of ignorance.
This verse clarifies the causes and effects of karma. The first three lines concern the cause of karma; the final line concerns the effect of karma.
Furthermore, the first line refers to the object (*viṣaya*); the second and third lines refer to the faculty (*indriya*). Because the faculty grasps the object, karma is thereby established.
"Grains" refers to rice, hemp, millet, wheat, beans, and so forth. "Flowers" refers to pine, chrysanthemum, lotus, and so forth. "Fruits" refers to sugarcane, grapes, and other fruits.
"Alcohol" refers to that which is fermented from grains, wheat, flowers, fruits, and so forth, and which has the power to intoxicate a person.
"One must not drink, taste, or smell it": "drinking" means swallowing; "tasting" means tasting with the tongue; "smelling" means smelling with the nose.

There are those who become intoxicated after drinking, and there are those who also become intoxicated by tasting or smelling. Even if one does not become intoxicated by merely tasting or smelling, one fears that it may give rise to a gradual [addiction].
Because it is defiled, it is prohibited by the precepts and not permitted; nor may one give it to others.

This means that although one does not drink it oneself, one must not cause others to drink it either, as this would lead them to become deluded, lose their wisdom, and commit various evil deeds. Therefore, the Precept Sūtra states:
"A Bodhisattva should generate the wisdom of clarity and penetration in all sentient beings; yet instead, they further cause all sentient beings [to fall into confusion]."
This refers to those with perverted minds who increase the karma of ignorance. By drinking alcohol in the present life, they become inverted, confused, and deluded regarding their true nature;
in future lives, they will increase their state of darkness and lose the seed of wisdom.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Drinking alcohol leads to much negligence; in this life one is constantly deluded and forgets all matters, and is perpetually rebuked by the wise.
In future lives one remains perpetually dull-witted and loses many merits. For this reason, the person of keen wisdom—"

One is free from all the faults of drinking alcohol. Furthermore, it is said: "If a person can renounce alcohol and correctly practice the Dharma and the precepts, they will reach the supreme place—the realm where there is neither death nor birth."
"Alcohol is the gateway to all evils; it produces every kind of transgression. To leave the home life and yet drink alcohol is not to be a seed of the Buddha’s Śākya lineage.
This verse clarifies the faults and afflictions of alcohol; it is not appropriate for those who are sons of the Śākyas. The preceding verse clarified [the increase of] self and others.
Karma. Now, this verse clarifies the cultivation of evil within one's own person. Regarding the statement that "alcohol is the gateway to all evils":
the meaning of a "gateway" (dvāra) is that which enables passage for entry and exit. This means that for one who drinks alcohol, evils such as greed, hatred, and delusion enter through it;
while crimes such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying exit by way of it. Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Formerly, there was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who..."
By nature he was benevolent and virtuous; he had received and upheld the five precepts, observing them with single-minded diligence and never transgressing them.
