Later, on one occasion, being overcome by thirst, he saw a vessel containing what appeared to be water but was actually wine. He took it and drank it, thereby violating the precept against intoxicants. A neighbor’s rooster entered his house; he stole and killed it for food.
When the neighbor’s daughter came searching for the rooster and entered his room, he forcibly compelled her to engage in sexual intercourse. The neighbor...
To report to authorities, to refuse to acknowledge, and to speak with deceit—these five precepts are all transgressed because of alcohol; therefore, it is called the gateway to all evils.
Regarding the commission of various faults, the *Śrāmaṇerikā-śīla-sūtra* states that there are thirty-six faults of alcohol.

Losing one’s way, ruining one’s family, endangering one’s person, and losing one’s life—all of these arise from this. It drags one east and pulls one west; it holds one to the south and fixes one to the north.
One cannot recite the sutras, does not revere the Triple Gem, treats teachers and friends with contempt, and is unfilial toward one’s parents.

The mind becomes obstructed, leading to ignorance life after life and failing to encounter the Great Way. Because the mind lacks discernment, one must therefore abstain from drinking alcohol. Desiring...
Having departed from the five aggregates, the five desires, and the five hindrances, one attains the five supernormal powers and achieves deliverance from the five realms of existence;
for this reason, one does not drink alcohol. To leave the household life and yet drink alcohol is to be no follower of the Buddha’s lineage.

Since alcohol causes one to lose the Way, ruins the family, endangers the person, and brings about the loss of life, even wise laypeople who observe the five precepts as upāsakas renounce it; how much more so for those who have left the household life?
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Son of the Dharma King, does not abandon us. If one were to abandon him, one would not be a disciple of the Buddha.
Therefore, the Buddha said: "If you say, 'I am a disciple of the Buddha,' you must not drink alcohol—not even a single drop on the tip of a blade of grass.
However, if there is a grave illness or a chronic disease that cannot be cured by other medicines..."
If the illness does not subside and a physician instructs one to use alcohol as medicine, there is no offense. However, one must not consume it under false pretenses of illness.

One’s faith and precepts must remain unimpaired. One should abandon all inverted karmas, eliminate the hindrances, cultivate mindfulness and wisdom, and achieve the perfection of the five faculties and five powers.

This verse concerns the four categories of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). For one who wishes to realize unsurpassed *bodhi*, the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment must be taken as the priority.

To eliminate the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and outflows (*āsrava*), one must take precepts (*śīla*) as the foundation. Yet, the Path does not progress without wisdom (*prajñā*), and precepts do not arise without faith (*śraddhā*).
Thus, it is known that faith is the source of the Path and the mother of merit; it gives birth to the immeasurable roots of giving, morality, learning, and wisdom.

The powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, the liberations, the samādhis, and the noble wealth—such is the noble wealth. It cannot be protected without the precepts; therefore, the Vinaya-mūla states:
"Those who wish to protect the noble wealth of the Dharma, listen as I speak to you, O assembly. To state it briefly:
the noble fruits of the Three Vehicles and the myriad practices of the Six Perfections all emerge from this. A practitioner who has left the household life out of faith should follow [the precepts]."
The Tathāgata’s prohibitions and precepts provide both natural restraint (*pratikṣepa-śīla*) and formal protection (*vidhi-śīla*); this is what is meant by being "without deficiency or transgression.

Because there is no deficiency or transgression, concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) arise from it; thus it is said that "perverted karmas are all abandoned. These refer specifically to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇāni*):

first, the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), which means coveting worldly wealth, beauty, objects, and the like; second, the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*), which refers to [the mind] toward disagreeable objects...

1. The hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*): This refers to the arising of a mind of anger. 2. The hindrance of sloth-and-torpor (*styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa*): Torpor (*styāna*) is the state of the mental consciousness being drowsy and heavy;

torpidity (*middha*) is the state of the five sense faculties being darkened and obscured. 3. The hindrance of restlessness-and-regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*): Restlessness (*auddhatya*) is the improper agitation of body and mind;

regret (*kaukṛtya*) is the subsequent distress and affliction over what has been done. 4. The hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*): Due to the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*), one fails to distinguish between the true and the false; because of this hesitation and indecisiveness, it is called doubt.
These five factors shroud the mind of the practitioner, preventing the arising of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and all other wholesome dharmas;

therefore, they are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*). Mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*): mindfulness refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and wisdom refers to the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*). Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness:
first is the contemplation of the impurity of the body, which means contemplating one's own body and the bodies of others from head to foot as a collection of filth and impurities.
It is filled [with impurities]. Sentient beings, through their inverted views, grasp it as pure and give rise to craving and attachment; therefore, one is led to contemplate the body as impure.
Second, one contemplates that feeling is suffering. "Feeling" refers to the act of receiving and grasping;

that is to say, sentient beings, through their inverted views, falsely perceive the six sense objects through the six sense organs as pleasure, not realizing that this so-called pleasure is the cause of suffering; therefore, one is led to contemplate feeling as suffering.

Third, contemplate that the mind is impermanent. This means that the substance and nature of this conscious mind are subject to flux; from moment to moment it grasps at objects, arising and ceasing without pause.
Sentient beings, through their inversions, cling to it as being permanent; therefore, one is led to contemplate the impermanence of the mind. Fourth, contemplate that all phenomena are without self.
This means that all phenomena, whether wholesome or unwholesome, fundamentally lack a self. Why is this? If [it were] wholesome...
If the dharma were the self, then unwholesome dharmas would have no self. If unwholesome dharmas were the self, then wholesome dharmas would have no self.
Yet sentient beings falsely reckon that "I" can perform wholesome deeds or unwholesome deeds, grasping at it as a sovereign master.
Therefore, he causes them to contemplate that all phenomena are without self.

These four dharmas all arise because sentient beings give rise to the four inversions regarding the body composed of the five aggregates—form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. They give rise to the inversion of purity regarding form; the inversion of pleasure regarding feeling;
the inversion of self regarding perception and mental formations; and the inversion of permanence regarding the mind. The Tathāgata causes them to cultivate this contemplation so that...
They are called the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) because they eliminate the four inversions. "Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) refers to the contemplation that is capable of observing;

"foundation" (*upasthāna*) refers to the objects that are observed. As for the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*): first, the elimination and severance of unwholesome states that have already arisen;

second, the prevention of the arising of unwholesome states that have not yet arisen; third, the production of wholesome states that have not yet arisen; and fourth, the increase and expansion of wholesome states that have already arisen. This...
Regarding why all four are called "right efforts" (*samyak-pradhāna*): "right" means not being deviant, and "effort" means not being indolent;
this refers to practicing these four dharmas with single-minded diligence and vigor. Regarding the five faculties (*pañcendriya*):

first is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), which means having faith in the right path and the factors conducive to the path, and being able to give rise to all untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis. Right...

The Path consists of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), while the aids to the Path consist of the five methods of mental abiding (*pañca-viṣkambhaṇa-citta*). Second is the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*):

this means that once one has faith in the teachings of the primary and auxiliary paths, one redoubles one's exertion and strives diligently without ceasing. Third is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*):

this means that by recollecting only the primary and auxiliary path teachings and maintaining mental visualization, one prevents the mind from falling into error and thus attains entry [into the Path]. Fourth is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).

The faculties (*indriya*). This refers to the dharmas of the primary and auxiliary paths that collect the mind; the mind is thus in accord with tranquil concentration (*samādhi*) and is not distracted or agitated.

The five faculties of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). This refers to the wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). When this wisdom is embraced by the dharmas of concentration, its internal nature illuminates itself spontaneously, without depending on knowledge from another;
this is what is called "wisdom. The practitioner first cultivates the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness; although it is a wholesome sprout...
The sprouts have barely emerged, yet the roots have not yet grown; fearing that these wholesome shoots might easily perish, one now cultivates five dharmas to cause the wholesome roots to arise.

Therefore, they are called "roots. As for the "five powers," their names are identical to the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), but they differ in that their power is able to destroy unwholesome dharmas and accomplish wholesome ones.
This means that although the wholesome roots have arisen, evil has not yet been eliminated; thus, one must further practice them so that—
Because the faculties (*indriya*) can be overcome and broken by evil, they are further established as "powers" (*bala*). Faith is able to sever doubt and is not moved by partiality or deviance.
Diligence (*vīrya*) is able to eliminate physical and mental laziness and accomplish supramundane dharmas.

Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is able to destroy all false conceptions and achieve all merits of supramundane right mindfulness. Concentration (*samādhi*) is able to destroy all distractions and give rise to...
Regarding the meditative concentrations on all phenomena and principles, "wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
It illuminates all dharmas, is able to eliminate false and deluded attachments, and shatters the wisdom of those who are biased or limited.

If a practitioner wishes to cultivate mindfulness and wisdom, they must distance themselves from inverted karma, eliminate the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and outflows (*āsrava*), and close the gates to all evils. When mindfulness and wisdom increase in clarity, then the faculties [will flourish].
The power is accomplished. Thus ends the explanation of the fifth precept.
To wear, apply, or smear incense—whether as powder or paste—and to possess flower garlands and jeweled necklaces, using various ornaments to adorn the body:
all such acts violate the prohibitions of a śrāmaṇera.
This verse clarifies the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), the adorning and the adorned, and the transgressor and the transgression.

"Incense" (*xūn*) and "ornaments" (*pèi*), as well as various other decorations, refer to the tangible object (*spraṣṭavya-viṣaya*) that is adorned. The body is the sense faculty (*kāyendriya*) that performs the adorning;
it is also the person who commits the transgression. "Prohibitions" (*jìn*) refer to the offenses that are transgressed. "Incense" means burning famous incense to perfume the body and one's clothing.
"Requisites and so forth. "Wearing" (*pei*) refers to wearing or fastening [ornaments]. "Anointing" (*tu*) refers to using powdered incense to smear and wipe the body and clothing.

"Flower garlands" (*huaman*) refers to stringing flowers together to form a wreath for adorning the head and body. "Necklaces" (*yingluo*) refers to connecting the seven precious gems as ornaments to adorn the body and neck.
"Various adornments of the body" refers to using various types of damask, gauze, silk, and *can-kou* (silk produced by silkworms).
As for wearing garments such as finger rings and armlets to adorn the body—these all violate the prohibitions of a śrāmaṇera.

A son of the Śākya shaves off his hair and beard, discards ornaments, contemplates the impurity of the body, reflects on the impermanence of the world, maintains few desires and knows contentment, wears coarse cloth, and dons robes made of discarded rags. How can one contravene one's own original faith and instead succumb to greed?

Incense, flowers, necklaces, and other ornaments for adorning the body involve harming living beings and violating compassion; they contravene the Buddha’s clear prohibitions, and one incurs guilt with every act.
Therefore, it is said that these all violate the precepts of a śrāmaṇera.
Abandoning the conduct of pride and negligence, Not clinging to the dust of the world, One cultivates the bases of psychic power and the six supernormal knowledges to adorn oneself.

This verse describes the cultivation of concentration free from attachment: the first two lines concern freedom from attachment, while the latter two lines concern the cultivation of concentration. "Abandoning pride..."
Regarding "transcending conduct that does not cling to worldly dust": the aforementioned worldly ornaments for the body are the root of arrogance and negligence;
they obstruct progress in the untainted noble path and can further defile the practitioner's mind.
Therefore, they are called "worldly dust. As for "cultivating the bases of psychic power," these are the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), which refers to what is practiced.
The Dharma of these [bases of power]: all wishes shall be fulfilled accordingly. First is the base of power of desire (*chanda-ṛddhipāda*):

this means that regarding all dharmas one practices, if there is no heart of aspiration and desire, the matter will certainly not succeed; if one possesses aspiration and desire, then whatever meditative observation of the foundations of mindfulness one intends to cultivate will all be accomplished.
Second is the base of power of mindfulness (*smṛti-ṛddhipāda*): this means that mindfulness is focused intently upon the object of observation.

The state of single-mindedness and right abiding. If one is not single-minded, the contemplation of phenomena will be interrupted; if one can be single-minded, all that is wished for will be attained.

Third is the basis of psychic power of diligence (*vīrya-ṛddhipāda*). This means that the practitioner focuses exclusively on contemplating the principle without allowing any distraction or intermingling;
therefore, it is called diligence. However, regarding all dharmas that are cultivated, if there is no diligence, the matter [will not be accomplished].
It will certainly not be accomplished. If one can be diligent, all that is wished for will be attained. Regarding the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) based on contemplation:
this means that if one contemplates the principles of what has been cultivated, the mind does not wander, and all that is wished for will be attained.

Regarding "adorned by the six supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*): *abhijñā* refers to the superknowledges; "spiritual" (*shen*) refers to the divine mind, and "power" (*tong*) refers to the nature of wisdom. It is innate—
Wisdom that penetrates and illuminates without obstruction is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*). First is the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*):

it can see sentient beings of the six realms as they die here and are born there, perceiving the signs of their suffering and joy, as well as all the various forms and colors of the world without any hindrance.
Second is the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-abhijñā*): it can hear the voices of sentient beings of the six realms, whether expressing suffering, joy, grief, or happiness.

1. The supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*), which perceives all sounds, including those of the world and various vocalizations. 2. The supernormal power of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣur-abhijñā*), which perceives all forms, including those of the world and subtle or coarse manifestations. 3.
The supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna-abhijñā*), which is able to know the thoughts and mental activities of sentient beings within the six realms of existence. 4.

The supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*), which is able to know the past lives of oneself and others, from one lifetime up to hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, as well as the deeds performed therein. 5. The supernormal power of mastery over bodily form (*rddhi-viṣaya-abhijñā*), which is able to...

One can manifest transformations at will, becoming either large or small; one flies with mastery, unimpeded by mountains or seas, vanishing here and appearing there, or vanishing there and appearing here.
Sixth is the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*). "Outflows" refers to the afflictions of views and thoughts within the three realms.
When these afflictions are completely severed, one no longer undergoes birth and death within the three realms and attains supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

The first four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) belong to concentration (*samādhi*); since supernatural powers arise from concentration, the six supernormal powers are manifested by relying upon the four bases of power. The four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) constitute wisdom (*prajñā*).

If one does not apply diligent effort in the contemplation of wisdom, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) will not be established, and one will instead invite distraction and agitation, like a lamp in the wind. Now...

Cultivate the power of mastery (*ṛddhi*). Just as in a sealed chamber, when concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are established in peace and equilibrium, the wholesome dharmas of the five faculties—whether in semblance or in reality—arise spontaneously.
It is like when the yin and yang are harmonized, and all seeds sprout from their roots.
Therefore, if the practitioner abandons arrogance and negligence, the faculties and powers of mindfulness and wisdom will be perfected. Not...

When one is detached from worldly dust, the five hindrances are naturally eliminated; when one cultivates the powers of mastery (*ṛddhi*), the six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) arise simultaneously.
To attain these six supernormal knowledges that adorn both body and mind, one must discard the various worldly ornaments.
Thus, the *Śrāmaṇerikā-śīla-sūtra* says: "To eliminate the six decays (*ṣad-vyasanāni*), take the precepts as fragrance; seek to recite the profound Dharma, regarding it as the ultimate reality. (3)
The twelve marks serve as his necklace; the various secondary characteristics planted by his virtue serve as his robes.
He vows to attain the six unimpeded supernormal powers and to guide others through the six perfections. This concludes the explanation of the sixth precept.
Singing, dancing, performers, and musicians; lutes, harps, flutes, and pipes; board games and gambling—none of these shall be practiced.
Nor shall one go to witness or listen to them. These two offenses are both not light.
Without clinging to various views or what is seen and heard, the seven factors of enlightenment will manifest before one.
This verse concerns the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). The first preceding verse clarifies "self-action.

The first phrase of the subsequent verse clarifies "action by another," while the second phrase defines the offense. The final two phrases clarify that when the faculties do not adhere to their objects, the *bodhicitta-samādhi* manifests spontaneously.
"Singing" refers to the production of songs from the mouth; "dancing" refers to the performance of dances with the body.
The term "singers and courtesans" (*chàngjì*) is a general designation for musicians. The ancient *qín* was three feet six inches and six *fēn* in length;
it was wider in the front and narrower at the back, with a waist four inches wide, circular on top and square at the bottom, featuring five strings and thirteen frets.
Later, King Wen added two strings, making seven in total. The original construction of the *sè* consisted of fifty strings, but later it was split so that only half were used.
The *xiāo* is made by binding small bamboo tubes together. The large version consists of twenty-three tubes and is fourteen inches long;
the small version consists of sixteen tubes and is twelve inches long. The *dí* is made from a hollow bamboo cylinder, fourteen inches long, with seven holes.
The *qiāngdí* (Qiang flute) has three holes. *Qíjú* (chessboard) refers to the board game for playing chess as it is known today. There are two kinds of chess: first, *tuánqí* (round chess);
second, *xiàngqí* (elephant chess), so called because it was decorated with ivory. *Bó* refers to gambling games, wherein one seizes the wealth and goods of others.
*Sài* refers to moving the pieces so that they block one another to determine victory or defeat. None of these activities should be practiced.

This means that when a *śrāmaṇera* leaves the household life, it is fundamentally for the purpose of abandoning worldly indulgence and diligently practicing with exertion in the hope of attaining *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, one should not engage in dancing, singing, or the like. Thus, as for going to observe or listen: observing refers to the faculty of the eye (*cakṣur-indriya*), and listening refers to the faculty of the ear (*śrotra-indriya*).
Consequently, going there demonstrates that one is not without intention; however, if one passes by such a place on the road without intentional purpose, there is no fault.

Regarding "viewing and listening": there is no offense. As for the two offenses being equally not light, this means that both acting oneself and going to view or listen result in the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).
Regarding "not being attached to what is seen or heard," this refers to the two faculties of eye and ear; they are not defiled by the aforementioned objects (*viṣaya*) such as sounds and forms.

However, seeing belongs to the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), and hearing belongs to the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*); because the faculties encounter their respective objects, consciousness arises.
Birth. Consciousness has the function of discernment; that is, it is able to discern whether sensory objects are beautiful or foul, wholesome or unwholesome, and so forth.

Regarding "the seven factors of enlightenment appearing before one": the seven factors of enlightenment are also called the seven limbs of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). "Intention" (*manas*) here refers to right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).

"Awakening" (bodhi) refers to the clear comprehension of whether the dharmas one practices are authentic or spurious. First is the awakening of the investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*):

the practitioner observes all dharmas with wisdom, discerning the authentic and discarding the spurious, so as not to take what is erroneous. Second is the awakening of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*):
"purity" means being unmixed; "progress" means being uninterrupted. The practitioner clearly realizes that practices which do not lead to the cessation of suffering are of no benefit.
Furthermore, within the True Dharma, one applies oneself with single-minded devotion and without interruption. Third is the awakening of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*):
this refers to the mind’s accord with the True Dharma, whereby one attains joy; one awakens to the realization that this joy arises from the True Dharma and does not arise from perversion.
Fourth is the awakening of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): this refers to the awakening that removes afflictions, delusive thoughts, and false phenomena, [revealing] what is truly real.

One thereby causes the roots of goodness to increase. Fifth is the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*): this means clearly realizing that dharmas are false and unreal, and having abandoned them, never again feeling regret.

Sixth is the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): this means that when the practitioner gives rise to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), they clearly realize all the dhyānas so that afflictions and delusive thoughts do not arise.
Seventh is the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*); "mindfulness" here refers to recollection; this means that the practitioner—
When practicing the various methods of the Path, one must skillfully awaken to them and always ensure that concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are balanced.

Among the factors of enlightenment, the three—discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), diligence (*vīrya*), and joy (*prīti*)—belong to wisdom; the three—tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and concentration (*samādhi*)—belong to concentration; and the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti*) belongs to both concentration and wisdom.
By practicing these seven factors of enlightenment, the practitioner enters the Noble Path. Therefore, the practitioner practices...

In practicing, one must distinguish between the true and the false; thus, one will not mistakenly grasp at sense objects. Regarding all that is unreal within the world—what is seen or heard—one shall forever abandon it.
With single-minded diligence, one shall find self-delight through the joy of dhyāna and the bliss of the Dharma;

therefore, this is called "manifesting before one. The *Śrāmaṇerikā-śīla-sūtra* says: "Constantly cultivate your own person, practice the True Dharma accordingly, and do not engage in what is perverse."
Practice. With single-minded devotion, take refuge in the Buddha; recite the sutras and practice with rectitude, taking this as the joy of the Dharma.

Thus ends the explanation of the seventh precept. Regarding beds, couches, and various seats: one is not permitted to make them of excessive size. Their height should be no more than one chi and six cun, and their width and length should likewise not exceed these limits.
One must not use carvings, lacquer, or silk curtains, nor exquisite woolen rugs, cushions, or coverlets.
"Those who are negligent and do not follow the teachings / Shall incur guilt even while sitting or lying down.
This verse concerns the rules for bedding. The first verse clarifies the dimensions of the bed; the second verse, its first two lines, clarifies that the object is not the substance itself.
The latter two phrases establish the offense by contradicting the teachings. "Bed" (*śayana*) refers to wooden beds, rope beds, beds with straight legs, or beds with curved legs;
a bed that is narrow and long is called a *tata*. "Various seats" (*āsana*) refers to high seats, low seats, large seats, and small seats.
This extends even to bathing benches and the like that exceed the proper measure. That is to say, they exceed sixteen *śaṅkhas* (cubits) in length and breadth.

Regarding the height of one *śaṅkha* and six *vitastis*: this refers to excluding the base of the bed; the legs should be eight fingers of the Tathāgata in height. Eight fingers of the Tathāgata [equals the standard unit of measurement].
The length for an adult is one *cubit* (*hasta*), which corresponds to one foot five inches by the Zhou standard. The *Śāstra* states that one finger-breadth of the Buddha is two inches.
As for the statement that "it should not be overly large," this means it should be appropriate to the person's own body. As the *Āgama Sūtra* says:
"Your Majesty’s feet are sixteen inches long, which is not tall; four feet wide, which is not broad; and eight feet long, which is not large.
Anything exceeding these measurements is called a high, wide, and large bed. Furthermore, there are eight kinds of beds: first, gold beds; second, silver beds."
1. The three-pronged bed; 2. The four-cornered bed; 3. The Buddha’s bed; 4. The Pratyekabuddha’s bed; 5. The Arhat’s bed; 6. The Teacher-monk’s bed.
The first four are distinguished by their material substance as being noble, and it is improper to sit upon them. The latter four are distinguished by the status of the person [to whom they belong].

Even if the ground is covered with mats intended for a person of high status, it is still not permissible to sit upon them. Regarding "carved and lacquered" (diaoqi): this refers to items that have been carved and decorated with lacquer and colors;
because such objects are precious and expensive, they are also termed "high and broad. Therefore, the Vinaya states: "There are two kinds of high beds and low beds.
First, those that are physically low are called 'low. Second, those that are coarse and inferior are also called 'low. There are likewise two kinds of high [beds]: those that are high..."
Great fame is "high"; exquisite beauty is also called "high. Exquisite beauty refers to such things as carvings, engravings, lacquer, colors, gold, silver, ivory, and horn;
it includes fine silks, curtains, and superior woolen rugs, blankets, and coverlets. These are not appropriate for those who have left the household life to seek liberation from birth and death;
rather, they are what kings, ministers, and worldly people prize. They serve only to indulge the illusory body and increase the karma of outflows (*āsrava*). Therefore—
The Buddha did not permit it. If one willfully violates the Buddha’s regulations—whether sitting or reclining—one immediately incurs the offense of breaking the precepts.
Having renounced the world, one should eliminate arrogance and self-indulgence, subdue the conceit of "I" and "mine," tread the Eightfold Noble Path, and sit upon the couch of the Dharma-emptiness.

This verse concerns the path of cultivation that is free from faults and the realization that all phenomena are empty. "Arrogance" (māna) is defined as relying on oneself to treat others with contempt;
its essential nature is loftiness, and its function is the production of suffering. It is because of this that one transmigrates through birth and death, undergoing immeasurable suffering.

The reason sentient beings are unable to attain liberation from birth and death is entirely due to their arrogance, self-indulgence, and egoism (*asmimāna*). The fundamental purpose of leaving the household life is to escape [this].
To transcend birth and death, one must certainly restrain arrogance and indulgence, and subdue the afflictions of ego-clinging (*māna*).
If one seeks to cultivate and realize the Noble Path while allowing afflictions to persist without cessation, it is like steaming sand in an attempt to cook rice.

To "tread upon" the Eightfold Noble Path means to practice and advance along it. The Eightfold Noble Path is also called the Eightfold Holy Path; it is divided into eight factors, the first being Right View (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).
First is Right View, which means seeing the principle of the Four Noble Truths; it is capable of destroying the false views of existence and non-existence.
Second is Right Intention, which means reflecting with right mindfulness and observation to cause right contemplation to increase.

Third is Right Speech, which means constantly restraining verbal karma through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) and remaining far removed from speech that is false and unreal. Fourth is Right Action, which means restraining the mind and abiding in...
1. Pure Right Action: This means severing all deviant and deluded conduct. 2. Five Right Livelihoods:

This refers to abandoning the four types of wrong livelihood and constantly seeking alms for one's own sustenance. 3. Right Diligence: This refers to cultivating morality, concentration, and wisdom with single-minded devotion and focused application.

There is no interruption. Seventh is right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*): it means being mindful of the factors of the path—both primary and auxiliary—consisting of morality, concentration, and wisdom, thereby being capable of progressing toward *nirvāṇa*.
Eighth is right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*): it means gathering all distractions so that body and mind become tranquil.
It abides correctly in the principle of true emptiness and is definitively immovable. These eight are collectively termed the "Right Path" (*samyak-mārga*);
"right" (*samyak*) signifies that which is not deviant. Now, these eight dharmas do not proceed by relying on partiality or deviation; therefore, they are called "right."
This is that which the noble ones and sages traverse to reach Nirvana; therefore, it is called the Path (*mārga*).

From the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, up to this eightfold noble path—these are known as the seven categories of the Dharma-gate.
Combined, they constitute the thirty-seven factors of the path (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), which are for all practitioners.
It is the ladder for entering the path through spiritual practice. As for "sitting upon the empty seat," sitting is that which relies [upon it], and the seat is that which is relied upon.
By means of this, the practitioner is able to cultivate right view and contemplate and examine worldly affairs.

To abandon falsehood and unreality, to suppress arrogance, and to practice right livelihood; to apply single-minded diligence toward the dharmas that assist the Path, whereby body and mind become tranquil;
and upon seeing the principle of the Truths, to abide in true emptiness without wavering—this is called "sitting upon the couch of dharma-emptiness.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "Taking dharma-emptiness as one's seat. This explains the eighth precept.
It is finished.
For all who have gone forth from the household life, they must not eat after midday; if they chew or consume food at an improper time, the Tathāgata has severely rebuked them.
This verse clarifies the characteristics of consuming, chewing, maintaining, and violating [the precepts]. The first half of the verse clarifies maintenance; the second half clarifies violation.
"Those who have left the household life" refers to the five groups of renunciants. "Not eating after midday" means that once the sun has passed the meridian line, one must not eat.
"Consuming or chewing at an improper time" refers to the time when the light of dawn appears.
"Up until midday": "Non-time" refers to when the sun has passed the western meridian until the appearance of the dawn light has not yet emerged;
this is not the time for a son of the Śākya to receive food, hence it is called "non-time. "Consuming" refers to eating rice, parched grain flour, congee, cakes, and so forth.

"Chewing" refers to eating fruits, melons, vegetables, and the like. If there is a cause for illness, it is permitted to take medicinal pills, powders, decoctions, or ointments, even including all things salty, bitter, sour, or pungent, as well as ashes, soil, excrement, or urine—anything unfit to be considered food, such as ginger, cinnamon, oil, or vinegar.
Furthermore, it is not permitted to eat these in large quantities. If one suffers from the afflictions of hunger or thirst, it is permitted to consume sugar, honey, and the five fruits.
8. Regarding the five fruits for syrups (*pānaka*): first, *harītakī*; second, *bibhītaka*, which resembles a peach and is not found in this region;
third, *āmalaka*; fourth, *pippalī*; fifth, *marica*. Regarding the eight syrups: first, pear;
second, *jambūphala*, shaped like a melon and not found in this region; third, sour jujube; fourth, sugarcane; fifth, *bījapūra*; sixth, lotus-root juice.
Seventh is *pālusa*, which resembles the fruit of the *yǐngǔ* (blackberry); it is not found in this region. Eighth is *pútáo* (grape).
These eight kinds [of fruits] are used to press into a juice, filtered through a cloth bag, and placed in a clean vessel; when it has become clear like the color of water, one may drink it.
As for other juices such as those from *jú* (tangerine), *yòu* (citron), *shíliú* (pomegranate), and *jiāozǐ* (banana), if they do not cause intoxication, they may likewise be used.
Liquids must be pressed clean and filtered; they must not be chewed or boiled as broth.

Nowadays, there are those who consume olives, honey-melons, honey-winter-plums, or honey-boiled yams outside of the permitted time for eating; this is truly contrary to the Dharma and should be corrected immediately.
If one suffers from a serious illness that cannot be cured by medicine and a physician instructs them to chew food, it should be given to them in a secluded place.
Once the illness has been cured, one must strictly abstain from such food. Unless it is a matter of life and death, one must by no means rely on a minor ailment as a pretext to eat;
doing so will only invite transgression and fault. The *Śrāmaṇerikā-śīla-sūtra* states:
"If a householder or a king offers food after midday, one must not eat it; this shall never be violated until death. Regarding the Tathāgata’s profound censure, the Buddha said: [text continues]
It is said: "One who eats at an improper time is a person who has broken the precepts; such a person is a thief who steals the property of the donor.
It is not the intention of the donor, and because the object has been lost, the donor gains no merit. Even the various Brahmins do not eat at an improper time."
Even the non-Buddhist brahmins do not eat such improper food; how much less should my disciples—who know the Dharma and practice the Dharma—act in this way?
Anyone who does so is not my disciple; they are thieves of the benefits of my Dharma, adherents of the doctrine of non-existence, and stealers of both name and food.
For even a single lump, a single handful, a morsel of salt, or a drop of vinegar, one will fall after death into the Hell of the Scorched Bowels and swallow hot [iron balls].
The iron ball emerged from hell and was reborn among pigs and dogs, where it ate various impurities;
it was then reborn as a malevolent bird, whose cries were strange to humans, and finally it was reborn as a hungry ghost within the latrine of a monastery, devouring filth and excrement.
For hundreds of thousands of millions of years, they will be reborn among humans as poor, lowly, and base individuals who are loathed by others;
whatever they say, people will not trust or believe. This is less grave than stealing the property of a single person.

Because it seizes and robs many people of their excellent field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) and cuts off the path to transcendence (*lokottaramārga*), this is a great thief; this is indeed [the cause of] starvation.
Demons are the dwelling places of sin. Those who partake [of offerings] at such times are, in fact, fields of merit;
they are renunciants; they are the true friends of devas and humans; they are the guides of devas and humans. As the Buddha has taught, how could one not observe the precepts?
"All classes of sentient beings / Are all greedy for the taste of food; / Wandering through the three realms, / They never for a moment leave their dependence on food.
This verse clarifies the cause of transmigration. Regarding "all classes of sentient beings are all greedy for the taste of food": all...
"Sentient beings" refers to those of the six realms and four modes of birth. The six realms are: devas, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
The four modes of birth are: womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born. All such sentient beings subsist by means of food. There are four kinds of food:

first, edible food in morsels (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). "Morsel" refers to a physical portion; its substance consists of fragrance, flavor, and tangibility. This includes rice, parched grain, beans, and so forth.
1. Food of edible morsels (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), such as meat soup and gruel. 2. Food of contact (*sparśāhāra*). "Contact" refers to the act of touching or encountering.

When the six consciousnesses encounter their respective objects, a mind of joy and pleasure arises; one naturally ceases to feel hunger, just as when men and women touch one another or when one watches plays and performances—through such sensory reception and attachment, one remains satiated throughout the day.
3. Food of volition (*manahsaṃcetanāhāra*). "Volition" refers to mental intention, which is the sixth consciousness. It consists of the volitional engagement with desirable objects.
It moistens and benefits the sense faculties (*indriya*), enabling the life-span to endure. This is like how humans, by thinking of food and drink, do not die;
it is also like fish, turtles, frogs, snakes, and so forth. Among the four nutriments, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the eighth [link], characterized by its sustaining power (*dhṛti-lakṣaṇa*).

Because it is supported by the influence of the first three nutriments, this consciousness increases and becomes predominant, thereby able to sustain the sense faculties and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Furthermore, the earth...
The sentient beings in the hells, as well as those in the formless realm—such as the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness—all take consciousness as their sustenance and use it as their food.
Regarding those who transmigrate within the three realms and do not for even a moment dwell apart from food, the Sūtra says:

"Sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death by means of these four kinds of nutriment. This refers to the three realms: the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). As for the desire realm...

The realm consists of the human world, the four destinies, and the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The form realm (*rūpadhātu*) consists of the four dhyāna heavens. The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) consists of the four spheres of emptiness.
All sentient beings wandering in saṃsāra within these three realms subsist by relying upon the four nutriments (*āhāra*);

if they were deprived of these four nutriments, their lives could not be sustained. Therefore, in the desire realm, edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) serves as nutriment; as for the two higher [realms]— *Note: The source text appears to be truncated at this point.*
Because the realms [of form and formlessness] lack the two objects of odor and flavor, the remaining three nutriments (āhāra) pervade all three realms;
therefore, it is said that "one dwells without even temporarily being free from nutriment. In the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"You should together focus your mindfulness on abandoning the four kinds of worldly nutriment and seek to procure the five kinds of supramundane nutriment: first, the nutriment of dhyāna-delight; second, the nutriment of aspiration."
Third is the food of mindfulness; fourth is the food of the eight liberations; fifth is the food of joy—these are the foods that transcend the world.
To sever the cause of saṃsāra, one should eliminate the food of ghosts and animals; by studying the meaning of the Buddha’s Middle Way, one attains the nine kinds of dhyāna.

This verse clarifies the severing of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the cultivation of realization. Regarding the desire to sever the causes of affliction, it is said that one should eliminate the consumption [of food] like that of ghosts and animals.

Since sentient beings take food as the cause of birth and death, and among those in birth and death none are more inferior than ghosts and animals, if one habituates oneself to their cause, one will inevitably invite their fruit.
Therefore, the Buddha established the precept to sever that cause, so that one may partake of food like the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The Sūtra states: "At dawn, the devas eat; at midday, the Buddhas eat; in the afternoon, the animals eat; at dusk, the ghosts and spirits eat.
Since inferior causes have been severed, superior fruits gradually become perfected. Furthermore, by not eating outside of the proper time, one obtains four benefits in the present life:
first, little drowsiness or sleep; second, freedom from the ailment of undigested food; third, physical lightness and tranquility; and fourth, the mind becomes easily [concentrated].

One attains meditative concentration; such are its benefits, and for this reason, midday meals are regulated. Regarding "learning the meaning of the Buddha’s Middle Way": "learning" means practicing and studying;

"middle" refers to the central correctness (*madhyama*), which signifies severing the opposition between the two extremes of existence and non-existence. One contemplates this present single thought-moment as being neither empty nor provisional, yet both empty and provisional.

Because one contemplates within this single thought-moment, within that one [thought]— [...]* *Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation). The ellipsis indicates the continuation of the original passage.*

Among all things, there is neither emptiness nor the provisional that is not the Middle. Because each of the three contemplations, in its own place, is able to transcend all dependencies, it is called the Middle Way.
Since all Buddhas and Tathāgatas constantly abide in the Middle Way, they are free from inopportune times.
Therefore, from the moment the World-Honored One was born in the royal palace until his parinirvāṇa, throughout the seventy-nine years in between, he never...

He once refrained from eating at improper times. Thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Because the World-Honored One is by nature free from eating at improper times, the Saṃgha originally follows the Buddha’s example;
remaining far removed from the two extremes, they do not eat at improper times. By doing so, one attains the nine types of dhyāna.

1. Samādhi of Self-Nature (*svabhāva-dhyāna*). This refers to a bodhisattva dwelling with single-minded concentration within the meditative state of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, based on all the mundane and supramundane virtues previously practiced.
Regarding the term "self-nature": it means that the dhyāna being cultivated contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the mind;
it is not obtained from without, but is the very samādhi that is inherently present as self-nature. 2. All... [text continues]

Dhyāna (meditative concentration). This means that by cultivating this dhyāna-samādhi, all dharmas—both those for one's own practice and those for transforming others—are encompassed without exception.
There are three types: first, the dhyāna of dwelling happily in wholesome dharmas; second, the dhyāna of producing the merit of samādhi; and third, [the dhyāna of the fruit of liberation].
The Dhyāna for Benefiting Sentient Beings. ○ Third, the Difficult-to-Cultivate Dhyāna. This refers to a meditative concentration that is not easily cultivated.
It has three types: first, one who has long practiced meditative concentration and attained mastery over the mind;

out of compassion for sentient beings, they relinquish the bliss of the first dhyāna and are reborn in the desire realm. Second, relying on this meditative concentration, they give rise to immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable...

They deliberate upon the various profound *samādhis*, which transcend those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Third, by relying on this meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one attains unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Fourth is the meditation of all gates (*sarvadvāra-dhyāna*). This means that all meditative concentrations emerge from these gates. There are four types:
first, with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), which is the first dhyāna; second, the dhyāna accompanied by joy (*prīti-sahagata-dhyāna*), which is...
The second is the *dhyāna* of joy (*sukha*). The third is the *dhyāna* accompanied by joy; this is the third *dhyāna*. The fourth is the *dhyāna* accompanied by equanimity (*upekṣā*);
this is the fourth *dhyāna*. Fifth is the *dhyāna* of virtuous persons (*satpuruṣa-dhyāna*). This refers to all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) which encompass everything;

it is that which is cultivated in common by beings of great capacity. It has nine types: first, the *dhyāna* without attachment to flavor (*āsvāda*); second, the *dhyāna* accompanied by a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*); third...
1. Dhyāna accompanied by compassion (*karuṇā*). 2. Dhyāna accompanied by sympathetic joy (*muditā*). 3. Dhyāna accompanied by equanimity (*upekṣā*). 4. Dhyāna of all practices (*sarvākāra-dhyāna*):
this refers to the Mahāyāna teachings on all practices, as there is nothing not included therein. There are thirteen types [of dhyāna]: 1. Wholesome (*kuśala*) dhyāna. 2.
Indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dhyāna for transforming others. 3. Higher-tier (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*) dhyāna. 4. Insight-tier (*darśanabhāgīya*) dhyāna. 5. For oneself and others...
Sixth is the dhyāna of right mindfulness. Seventh is the dhyāna of producing the merit of supernormal powers. Eighth is the dhyāna of the name-condition;

"name" refers to the characteristics of names, and "condition" refers to causal conditions. Ninth is the dhyāna of the meaning-condition; this refers to the causal conditions of the principles and meanings of all phenomena.
10. Dhyāna based on the sign of tranquility (*śamatha-nimitta*). 11. Dhyāna based on the sign of exertion (*pragraha-nimitta*). 12. Dhyāna based on the sign of equanimity (*upekṣā-nimitta*). 13.
Dhyāna of the ultimate truth of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra-paramārtha-dhyāna*). 7. Dhyāna for the removal of afflictions (*vighāta-prahāṇa-dhyāna*):

This refers to the cultivation of this concentration which is able to eliminate the various sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings; it is said to have eight types: 1. Dhyāna that is the basis for incantations (*mantra-adhiṣṭhāna-dhyāna*). 2. Removal... [text truncated]

1. The meditation of curing illness; 2. the meditation of clouds and rain; 3. the meditation of equal deliverance; 4. the meditation of great benefit; 5. the meditation of subduing; 6. the meditation of awakening; 7.

the meditation of equal action; 8. the meditation of happiness in this world and the next—meaning that by practicing this concentration, one can cause all sentient beings to obtain every kind of happiness in both the present and future lives. There are nine types [of these meditations]. First:
1. The dhyāna that tames sentient beings through the manifestation of supernormal powers (*ṛddhiprātihārya*). 2. The dhyāna that tames sentient beings by conforming to their speech. 3.

The dhyāna that tames sentient beings through the manifestation of instructions and admonitions (*anuśāsanīprātihārya*). 4. The dhyāna that reveals the miserable realms (*apāya*) to sentient beings who commit evil. 5.

The dhyāna that benefits sentient beings who have lost eloquence by providing them with eloquence. 6. The dhyāna that benefits sentient beings who have lost mindfulness by providing them with mindfulness. 7. [The dhyāna that benefits sentient beings who have lost concentration by providing them with concentration.]
1. The meditation for composing treatises free from error and sublime hymns of praise; 2. The meditation for causing the True Dharma to endure for a long time; 3.
The meditation for gathering in sentient beings through the benefit of the eight worldly arts and sciences; 4. The meditation for temporarily halting rebirth in the evil destinies by emitting light.

○ Ninth, the dhyāna of the purity of purity. This refers to relying on this concentration such that all afflictions, delusions, and karmic actions are completely severed and exhausted, thereby attaining the fruit of the purity of Great Bodhi; thus it is called "purity.
It is stated twice as "pure" because even the characteristic of purity cannot be apprehended. There are ten types: first, the worldly purity of purity.
1. Meditation that is untainted by relishing and undefiled; 2. Mundane meditation that is pure through purification; 3. Meditation that is pure through the purification of skillful means; 4.
Meditation that is pure through the purification of the fundamental [dhyāna]; 5. Meditation that is pure through the purification of superior progress within the fundamental [dhyāna].
Sixth is the pure meditation purified by the power of entering, abiding, and emerging; seventh is the pure meditation purified by the power of returning to equanimity;
eighth is the pure meditation purified by the power of performing supernormal feats; ninth is the pure meditation purified by being free from all views;
tenth is the pure meditation purified by the severance of afflictive and cognitive hindrances. These nine kinds of great meditations appear in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*.
This means that once Bodhisattvas have donned the great vow to benefit sentient beings, they must advance in the practice of profound and vast deeds.
Since there is no practice more profound or vast than meditative concentration (dhyāna), it is said that by mentioning "meditation," all such practices are subsumed.
This refers to the supreme and wondrous merits of Bodhisattvas when they attain the Way, turn the wheel of Dharma, and enter nirvana, as well as their contemplations.
The cultivation of the Dharma and the skillful means for benefiting sentient beings are all contained therein.

Therefore, when a Bodhisattva wishes to cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices, to gather all merit and wisdom, and to achieve the Unsurpassed Way, they should practice these nine kinds of great dhyāna.

These nine dhyānas are all derived from the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*). When the three contemplations are perfectly integrated, then within one there is all, and within all there is one; there is no emptiness.

There is nothing provisional that does not accord with the mean; this is what constitutes the Middle Way. Therefore it is said: "By studying the meaning of the Buddha’s Middle Way, one immediately attains the nine kinds of dhyāna.
This concludes the explanation of the ninth precept.
A śrāmaṇera shall not accept or store gold, silver, or precious treasures.
However, if a donor offers them for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and for the purpose of generating merit for that donor, he is permitted to accept and use them.
If he privately accumulates wealth for himself, he violates the prohibitions against worldly gain.
This verse describes the characteristics of observing and violating the precepts. The first two lines constitute prohibitions; the middle four lines provide permissions;
and the final two lines state that one incurs guilt by transgressing the prohibitions. Regarding "gold, silver, and precious objects": gold refers to both wrought and unwrought gold;
silver refers to both wrought and unwrought silver; "precious objects" refers to the seven treasures, coins, and the like. A śrāmaṇera [is not permitted to...]
Regarding "accepting and keeping": "accepting" means to take up; "keeping" means to maintain. As stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
"At one time, there was a bhikṣu who took a śrāmaṇera with him to visit his relatives. On the way, they passed through a vast wilderness.

Midway, a non-human being manifested in the form of a dragon, circumambulated the śrāmaṇera to the right, scattered flowers over him, and praised him, saying: 'Excellent! You have gained great and wholesome benefit.'"
When the bhikṣu had reached his relatives and was about to return, a relative’s wife said, "The road is long and there will be many shortages;
you may take this money and purchase whatever you require. The śrāmaṇera accepted it, tied it to the hem of his robe, and departed.
On the way, a non-human being saw the śrāmaṇera carrying the money walking behind the bhikṣu; he transformed himself into a dragon and came forward, circling the śrāmaṇera to the left.
The novice covered him with dust and said, "You have lost a great benefit. The novice then wept. The bhikṣu asked him, "Why are you weeping?
The novice replied, "I do not recall having committed any fault; I have been troubled for no reason. The teacher asked, "Is there something you are holding?
He answered, "I am carrying this money here. The teacher said, "Discard it. Once it was discarded, a non-human being (amanuṣya) again...
As in the previous case of making offerings, there are such faults that obstruct the Path and ruin one's virtue; therefore, the Buddha compared them to a great venomous serpent.
For this reason, he did not permit their acceptance or possession. As for the phrase "if there should be a donor who gives," the word "if" is used as a hypothetical expression;
"dāna" (檀) refers to giving, and "pāramitā" (越度) refers to transcending [to the other shore]. This means that if a donor is able to practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), then—
This means to cross over the ocean of suffering of poverty. Since he is able to practice giving, he thus crosses over the ocean of suffering;

as for the recipient of his gift, how could one begrudge it? To do so would constitute a tainted karma. One should instead perform meritorious deeds on his behalf and further offer them to the Triple Gem.
Therefore, one should accept [the gift]. If one does otherwise and keeps it privately, one commits a violation of the śrāmaṇera precepts.
One should not give rise to craving for any pleasure that is possessed; because of attachment, birth and death are never severed—this verse explains the root source of saṃsāra.
Regarding "one should not give rise to craving for any pleasure that is possessed": [this means] excluding...
Apart from gold, silver, money, and treasures, one must not be attached to any clothing, utensils, or other articles of enjoyment.
As for the reason that birth and death are not severed: it is because of attachment through greed; greed is the root of birth and death.
Like a fly clinging to saliva, craving is the source of outflows (*āsrava*). It is like a tortoise thinking of water; thus, if craving is not heavy, one will not be born in this Sahā world.
If one wishes to attain non-arising (*anutpāda*), one must sever the source of craving. Therefore, it is said that "the exhaustion of craving is *nirvāṇa*. This is precisely what is meant.
"Unstained by worldly gain, always practicing the conduct of few desires, the wealth of the noble Dharma increases daily;
one shall realize the wisdom of the Ten Powers.
This verse concerns the realization of the path through freedom from defilement. The practitioner is not defiled in body or mind by worldly fame and profit. Always...

Cultivating the practice of few desires and contentment, one then possesses faith, generosity, ethical discipline, learning, wisdom, shame, remorse, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.
Liberation, the various dhyānas and samādhis, and immeasurable, supreme, and wondrous dharmic riches increase day and night.
Because they increase and reach fulfillment through this, one shall realize the ten powers of a Tathāgata in the future.

First is the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible; that is to say, the Buddha can truly and accurately know all causes, conditions, and their resultant retributions. As it is said:

When one performs wholesome karma, one knows with certainty that a pleasant retribution will be obtained; this is called "knowing the possible" (*sthāna-jñāna*). If one performs unwholesome karma and yet obtains a pleasant retribution, such a thing is impossible;
this is called "knowing the impossible" (*asthāna-jñāna*). In these various ways, he fully and universally knows all things.
Second is the power of knowing the knowledge of karma (*karma-jñāna-bala*), which means that the Buddha knows the karmic conditions of all sentient beings in the past, future, and present.
He thoroughly and universally knows the karmic results and the places of rebirth. Third is the power of knowledge regarding the determination of meditative concentrations:

this refers to the Buddha’s knowing all dhyānas and samādhis with mastery and without obstruction, thoroughly and according to reality as they are, including their degrees of depth and sequence. Fourth is the power of knowledge regarding the faculties.
This refers to the Buddha’s true and universal knowledge of the superior or inferior faculties of all sentient beings and the magnitude of the fruits they attain.

Fifth is the power of knowing the inclinations (*jñāna-bala*): this refers to the Buddha’s knowledge of the various desires and pleasures of sentient beings, which differ according to their wholesome or unwholesome natures, as he knows them truly and universally.
Sixth is the power of knowing dispositions (*jñāna-bala*): this refers to the Buddha’s knowledge of the various elements and inherent natures (*dhātu*) of sentient beings in the world.
They are distinct. [The seventh is] the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading to various destinations as they truly are.

This means that the Buddha, with respect to the destinations reached by impure (sāsrava) actions within the six realms of existence, and the destination reached by pure (anāsrava) actions—namely, nirvāṇa—knows them all as they truly are. [The eighth is] the power of knowledge regarding the divine eye.
This means that the Buddha’s divine eye is purified; he sees all sentient beings at the time of death and at the time of birth, whether they are handsome or...

He knows beauty and ugliness as they truly are. He knows, without obstruction, the causal conditions of wholesome and unwholesome karma as they truly and universally are. Ninth is the power of knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*).
This means that the Buddha knows various past lives: from one life up to hundreds of thousands of millions of lives; from one eon up to hundreds of thousands of millions of eons.
He knows: "In that place I died and was born here; in that place I died and was born here. He knows their names, their clans, and what they drank.
He knows, as they truly are, the food [of beings] and the length of their lifespans. Tenth is the power of knowing the permanent eradication of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
This means that the Buddha knows, as they truly are, the permanent cessation and non-arising of all afflictions (*kleśa*) and other habitual tendencies.
These ten are collectively called "powers" because they represent the application of the Buddha’s realized, true knowledge that penetrates all things.
It is perfectly clear and distinct; nothing can destroy it, and nothing can surpass it. Therefore, it is called "power.
The great Bodhisattvas also partially attain this power of wisdom, yet because it is slightly inferior compared to that of the Buddha, they do not receive its name.

As explained above, the observance of precepts, the making of vows, the cultivation of the various factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and the nine kinds of great dhyānas are for the most part attained by Bodhisattvas.

The methods for self-cultivation and the transformation of others are now contained within these ten powers, which are the gateways to the Dharma attained by all Buddhas through their own practice and the transformation of others.

Therefore, one should know that it is impossible for a bodhisattva who upholds the precepts and makes vows to attain the great meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) without cultivating the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and eliminating all hindrances and afflictions.
Furthermore, without possessing these meditative concentrations, it is likewise impossible to realize the ten powers.

Because this is the case, the ninth stage, the pure meditation of complete purity, exhaustively severs all afflictions, delusions, and karmic actions, thereby attaining the fruit of the great bodhi of purity. This concludes the explanation of the tenth precept.
These ten prohibitory precepts: the first four are the root. Be careful not to lightly violate them and lose the nature of a śrāmaṇera.
To commit a grave offense is like having one’s head severed;
it does not permit receiving the bhikṣu or bodhisattva vows again, as one has no share in them whatsoever. As for the latter six, even if they are deficient...
Feeling deep shame, one should confess to the teacher and resolve never to commit it again; thus the categories of precepts will be restored to their full purity.

But for one who commits an offense without shame or remorse, conceals it rather than revealing it, the defilement of sin increases day and night, and they will eventually fall into the three evil realms.
Among these, four verses summarize the preceding ten precepts. The first line provides a general heading, while the subsequent lines provide specific summaries.
First, the natural precepts (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) are summarized; next, the prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) are summarized.

These ten prohibitory precepts range from the first, "not killing," to the last, "not accepting gold, silver, or precious objects. The first four are the roots, namely: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying.
The root of all precepts is like the roots of a tree; if they are destroyed, the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits all fall away.

It is the same with the *prakṛti-śīla* (inherent morality): if one violates even a single item, all others are lost. The nature of a *śrāmaṇera* is precisely the unmanifested (*avijñapti*) body of the precepts.
To commit a grave offense is like severing one's head; once the root is destroyed, it is as if a person’s head has been cut off, and they will never again...
Resurrection. Thus, the Sūtra says: "If one violates a grave precept among the ten precepts, it is impossible to receive the ten precepts again, or the bhikṣu precepts, or the bodhisattva precepts;
therefore, it is said that in all such cases, one lacks the portion [of the precepts]. From this, we know the nature of these precepts.
These [precepts] can serve as the foundation for the bhikṣu precepts, the bodhisattva precepts, and even for unsurpassed bodhi;

therefore, it is said: "Be careful not to lightly violate them. Regarding the latter six [precepts], which state that if there is a deficiency, one must feel deep shame and repent before the teacher, this refers to the six prohibitory precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*), ranging from not drinking alcohol to not accepting or possessing gold and silver. If one violates any of these, one must immediately...
Deeply feeling shame and remorse, one confesses and repents before the Upādhyāya or the Ācārya, vowing never to commit it again.

Thus, the essence of the precepts (śīla-samvara) is restored to its pure and perfect state. This differs from the first four categories of *prakṛti-sāvadya* (inherent offenses), which entail immediate expulsion upon commission and do not admit of repentance.
Regarding these inherent offenses, regardless of whether one has received the precepts or not, their nature is such that they are committed by the very act itself.
This is evil. It is not because the Buddha prohibits it that there is good or evil; by committing such acts, one falls into the three miserable realms.

However, if one has already received the Buddha’s precepts and violates them, one incurs the additional offense of transgressing those prohibitions. To speak of "prohibiting" (遮) refers to the Buddha’s act of forbidding.
It is not permitted for a śrāmaṇera to commit transgressions. Regarding those who have committed offenses yet feel no shame or remorse, conceal them, and do not disclose them:

this refers to those who violate prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada*), fail to give rise to a sense of shame and remorse, and, concealing their flaws, are unwilling to confess before others.
It is like grass covered by a basin; it grows day and night, and the offense is likewise.

Because the cause shifts, the fruit ripens, and one immediately falls into the three evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. Having finished explaining the ten precepts, I shall next explain the methods for practicing in accordance with the Vinaya.
Once a śrāmaṇera has received the precepts, there are further things he should not do; these are what are called "playing with weapons" and "riding vehicles at will.

This verse concerns the initial signs of following the methods of the Vinaya. The first two lines provide a general indication, while the subsequent lines list them specifically. [The subject is] the śrāmaṇera.
Regarding those who have already received the precepts, this excludes those whose physical form is not identical [to that of a monk]. Furthermore, there are things that should not be done:

with the exception of the aforementioned ten precepts, the various rules and regulations listed below contravene the practice of renunciation; therefore, it is not permitted for a *śrāmaṇera* to perform them.
As for the phrase "wielding weapons," the word "so-called" (*suǒwèi*) is a particle used to introduce a statement, serving as a framework for the subsequent names, phrases, and sentences.
"Leads" means to guide. "To dally" refers to playing or jesting. "Weapons" is a general term for bows, arrows, spears, lances, blades, axes, and the like.
"Riding vehicles at will" means to indulge one's desires by mounting carriages, horses, and so forth. The *Śrāmaṇerikā-śīla-sūtra* states:
"If one is not ill, one must not ride in carriages, on horses, or on elephants; one should instead practice lightness of movement. (8)
Using the mastery of inconceivable supernatural powers as their vehicle,
they cage and bind various flying birds, raise domestic livestock, play with and shoot at species of birds and beasts,
and watch the catching of fish and turtles.
This verse clarifies the causes and conditions for killing. "Cage" refers to a trap or enclosure; "binding" refers to tethering.
"Flying birds" refers to creatures that travel through the air. Regarding the "six domestic animals," these are horses, oxen, sheep, chickens, dogs, and pigs, which are raised by the laity.
Since the Way and secular life are in opposition, their keeping is not permitted. However, if they are kept for the purpose of knowing the time or for protection, their keeping is allowed.
Roosters and male dogs; those that fly are called birds, and those that run are called beasts. To play with them and kill them is a method of slaughter.

Fish and turtles are sentient beings of the aquatic realm. To watch their capture is to rejoice in the act of killing. The term "and so forth" refers to all sentient beings that move through water, on land, or in the air;
none of these may be watched being captured.
Burning mountains and blocking streams, Tilling the soil and plowing the fields, Planting the five grains and engaging in trade as merchants,
Learning extraordinary arts and crafts, Studying geomancy, medicine, divination,
and physiognomy to reveal good and ill fortune, Observing the stars and calculating the calendar, And discussing matters of state governance.
Engaging in worldly discourse, appraising the prices of various goods, contending with others for profit,
and rushing about in the four directions— seeking a livelihood through such wrong means, whether acting oneself or instructing others,
one violates all the precepts of a śrāmaṇera.
This verse refers to the four types of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*), which means sustaining one's life-force through unrighteous means. "To burn" means to incinerate.
"To dam" refers to obstructing the upper reaches of a stream with materials to cause the downstream waters to dry up, thereby harming aquatic life.
"Turbid waters" is a general term for the Yangtze, Yellow, Huai, and Ji Rivers, as well as streams and ditches. "To plow and dig" refers to the clearing and cultivation of fields.
"Earth" (di) is the same as "plowing" (geng). Furthermore, some say that the person is called "the plower" (geng) and the ox is called "the plow" (li).

According to this, when the world was first formed, non-glutinous rice grew from the earth without requiring human labor. Because people began to contend over and seize it, the rice gradually diminished.

They collectively established a Great Man-King (darenwang) to adjudicate for the multitude. From the time of the Great Man-King onward, the practice of plowing and digging gradually arose. If one follows the account of this land [China]...
Shennong fashioned wood into plowshares and bent wood into plow-poles, first teaching the people to plant the five grains.
This continued until Houji, the son of Emperor Ku, who was fond of cultivation and sowing; Shun consequently appointed him as the Minister of Agriculture, whereupon he invented the ox-drawn plow.

Regarding the five grains, they are treated like wine according to the prohibitions. Buying low and selling high is called "trading" (*fàn*); traveling while doing so is called "merchandising" (*shāng*), while sitting to do so is called "peddling" (*jiǎ*).
"Working for hire" means being employed by others. "Learning extraordinary arts and crafts" refers to learning and knowing the movements of the sun, moon, and five planets;

interpreting dreams; predicting earthquakes; understanding the speech of ghosts, birds, and beasts; divining signs of abundance or calamity; observing the conjunctions of the sun, moon, and five planets;
medicine; mathematics and calculation; divination; singing and dancing; performing music; and various other crafts and technical skills. Thus it is said.
Regarding the discourse on state affairs and worldly talk: "State" refers to the establishment of laws through correct principles; "affairs" refers to the implementation of those laws;
and that which is not the speech of the Sūtras or Vinaya is called "worldly talk. The Śrāmaṇerikā-śīla-sūtra states:
One must not discuss worldly affairs, nor speak of matters concerning kings, ministers, officials, or bandits; this is correct. Regarding the four types of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*):
first, "downward-facing food," which refers to cultivating fields and gardens, and compounding medicinal decoctions.
Second, "upward-facing food," which refers to gazing upward at the stars, the sun, the moon, wind, rain, thunder, lightning, and the study of divination and numerology.
The "mouth-food of the three directions" refers to fawning upon those of power and influence to act as intermediaries for all four quarters, using clever speech to pursue many gains.
The "mouth-food of the four intermediate directions" refers to studying various extraordinary arts, incantations, physiognomy, and divination, traveling in all directions to seek them out.
Burning mountains, blocking streams, plowing and tilling the soil, planting crops, and practicing medicine—these are the "lower mouth-foods. To study these is... [the text continues].

Practicing extraordinary arts, geomancy, divination, and physiognomy constitutes "feeding on the mouth. Observing the stars, calendars, and mathematics constitutes "feeding on what is above the mouth.
Discussing state affairs, worldly discourse, evaluating commodity prices, and roaming about in all four directions all belong to "feeding on the four quarters.
Engaging in trade, selling goods, working as a hired laborer for others, and competing for profit—all these are forms of wrong seeking; this extends even to mere jesting.

Carrying weapons, watching the catching of fish and turtles, and so forth, are all contrary to the Dharma; therefore, whether one does these things oneself or instructs others to do so, one violates the conduct of a śrāmaṇera.
A śrāmaṇera leaves the household life in order to cultivate the path and its practice, abandoning worldly affairs and dwelling in solitude and stillness.

Abandoning the four types of wrong livelihood, one should follow the four right teachings: first, dwelling in deep mountains and sustaining oneself with whatever roots, tubers, or fruits are obtained;
second, constantly practicing alms-gathering; third, food sent by donors; and fourth, pure food from within the Sangha.
These are the means by which a son of the Śākya maintains a pure livelihood, not seeking through wrong or evil means.
One who is not virtuous is unfit to be a friend; one who is not a sage is unfit to be a model. Do not associate with, nor draw near to, nor become intimate with those who are youthful.

This verse concerns the honoring of teachers and the selection of friends. It means that a friend must be a good companion, a teacher and model must be wise and enlightened, and those one draws near to must be of venerable virtue.
Do not associate with the young; as time passes, intimacy grows, and through gradual emotional attachment, one’s reputation is ruined and virtue lost. It all begins from this.
Whether at home or ordained, do not dwell in the same place as women; if you encounter them on the road, do not converse.
Nor shall one share a boat with them; correspondence and visits must be severed. Do not allow them to wash, cut, or tailor for you;
do not beg from them, nor lend to or give gifts to them.
If they should offer a gift, one should not accept it impulsively; even if one holds some other object, one must not examine it.
When he is requested to teach the Dharma, if there are elders present or those whom he respects, he may then give the teaching.
Having finished speaking, he should remain silent; he must not laugh with his teeth bared, nor should he perform any improper actions whatsoever.

This verse distinguishes between men and women, as well as those who have left the household life and those who remain within it. Women who have left the household life are the śrāmaṇerikās, śikṣamāṇās, and bhikṣuṇīs.
Women who remain within the household are the upāsikās, the wives of laymen, widows, virgins, and young girls.
